title: France v Fiji: Five takeaways as 'exquisite' Antoine Dupont stars but injury to key man creates 'crisis' ahead of Springboks showdown - Planet Rugby
content: Theo Attissogbe heading over for a try for France against Fiji. France ran in eight tries to beat Fiji 54-17 in Lyon, with Antoine Dupont exquisite at the base and Geoffrey Doumayrou’s new defence impressive, but the loss of key man Romain Ntamack leaves Fabien Galthié with a fly-half crisis of endemic proportions six days before the Springboks rumble into Paris. Nobody does a rugby opening ceremony quite like France, and with a stunning new Adidas kit, a sold-out Groupama Stadium and Dupont and Ntamack together in la charnière for the first time since March 2025, this had all the expectation and makings of a special night. Galthié had promised something spectacular, and for long stretches we got it: eight tries, a player of the match performance from Dupont that was as good as anything we’ve seen from him in a blue shirt in years, and an attacking sequence early in the second half, ignited by the Toulouse nine, that was like somebody flicking a light switch on. But it was also a match and a French side that, at times, delivered a lot less than it promised. It took the hosts 14 minutes to score, after a start that saw Ntamack’s kick-off go straight into touch, Théo Attissogbé fumble the first contestable and the first French lineout throw go in crooked, and even with the game won they kept shooting themselves in the foot at the set-piece, dropping four driving mauls in the second half and effectively crippling the same weapon that had earned them a penalty try in the first. Then there’s the injury list, which now includes Ntamack, off after 33 minutes with a suspected left shoulder subluxation. It was, in the final analysis, l’œuf du curé: very good in parts, bad in others, and the parts that weren’t will worry Galthié far more than the scoreline suggests. Fiji, for their part, looked transformed in structure and organisation since the summer’s 73-8 humbling at the hands of England. Jake White said before kick-off that he wanted defence, discipline and territory from his side, and he got one of the three; the other two will need work before Dublin. Dupont was exquisite tonight. With Ntamack gone and Maxime Lucu, a scrum-half by trade, moving to 10, France needed someone to run the game, and Dupont simply took it on himself, roaming across the field looking for space, throwing 75 passes, beating five defenders and having a hand in try after try: the cross-kick that started Jean-Baptiste Gros’s opener, the opening that sent Sipili Falatea back against the grain, a long left-handed pass to put Aaron Grandidier-Nkanang away, a lightning break and flip pass behind him for Yoram Moefana that covered 60 metres in a flash, and finally a try of his own off the back of a driving maul with two minutes left. He also won the ball back on the touchline for Attissogbé’s try. 18 months ago he was recovering from a ruptured anterior cruciate ligament, but tonight he looked like a man who’d never been away. World Rugby rankings: How Saturday’s Nations Championship and Nations Cup action affects the standings Outside Dupont, Moefana was something else, direct and powerful on both sides of the ball with 14 carries for 91 metres and six defenders beaten, whilst Grandidier-Nkanang is seriously quick and made 123 metres, the most on the pitch, with Attissogbé close behind on 112. Most importantly for France, their starting front-row was very, very good indeed. Gros made ten tackles without a miss, scored a try and smashed Fiji for a scrum penalty early in the second half, and Falatea is as good with ball in hand as any tighthead in the game, although his scrummaging only just held on, and next weekend he’ll have a much sterner task. Louis Bielle-Biarrey’s work rate was phenomenal despite Fiji shutting him down for an hour, and when he finally broke them open he set up Attissogbé’s try; he also spent time at first receiver for set-piece attack, as he does for UBB when Lucu plays at 10. François Cros made 14 tackles and was generally outstanding, but for one lapse, when Vinaya Habosi stepped him magnificently and left Cros grasping at thin air with nobody covering the backfield; miss one like that against South Africa and you are toast. Yet France’s back-row looked a tad unbalanced. Cros is a collision forward who does his best work alongside the ball-carrier rather than over the ball himself, and at eight he perhaps looked a little constrained; with Cameron Woki and Paul Boudehent on the flanks, France had no real jackal threat, nobody whose first instinct is to get his hands on the ball at the tackle, and as a result Fiji counter-rucked superbly, retaining 82 of their 83 rucks and winning seven turnovers to France’s three, with Kitione Salawa claiming his second straight after the break. The veteran Charles Ollivon came on for Florian Verhaeghe on 57 minutes to the biggest cheer of the night, and it’s pretty much a rugby fact that he is to Galthie’s France what Jamie Tartt is to Ted Lasso’s AFC Richmond,; a goal-hanging pest of the highest order. Within a minute he’d ripped the ball from a Fijian on the floor for Kalvin Gourgues’s try; by the 72nd he’d scored one himself, an absolute poacher’s finish from close range for his 20th Test try, a record for a French forward, and to cap his night he caught the lineout that launched Dupont’s final score. White will be happy with Fiji in some respects. Their press and shape were miles better than in July, their counter-rucking was outstanding, with Tevita Ikanivere leading from the front with 17 tackles, the most on the pitch, and Nathan Hughes, who beat seven defenders, produced his trademark pick-and-go straight through a ruck. Crucially, Fiji elected to keep the ball on the park; with France’s maul already producing a penalty try and a yellow card for Mesake Vocevoce, every kick to touch was an invitation to drive, so Fiji kicked long and infield instead, out-kicking France by 685 metres to 501 and holding them to 53-47 in territory. Opinion: Average All Blacks blunder on and why someone other than the Springboks will expose them The downside is that they barely attacked until the final quarter, carrying just 47 times all night, and the other two of White’s targets fell well short. Both of France’s first-half tries from close range came from Fijian penalties, and 29 missed tackles at 69 per cent is far too many against anyone, let alone Ireland next week. The late flourish was encouraging, with Habosi and Selestino Ravutaumada, after lovely interplay with Frank Lomani, matching France try for try over the last quarter of an hour, and it’s a sign of what this group can achieve once the structure White is building is in place. There’s a lesson in the numbers too: Fiji won the kicking metres, the ruck count and the turnover battle yet still lost by 37, which tells you how ruthlessly France turned possession into points in the red zone when they bothered to be accurate. One odd call deserves explaining, because it decided a try outcome and it left Fiji felt pretty aggrieved. A player can claim a mark only in his own 22, catching the ball cleanly direct from an opponent’s kick and calling “mark” as he does so, but the catch has to be completed, with the ball fully under control. When Dupont’s long pass sent Grandidier-Nkanang away and he kicked ahead, Vilimoni Botitu took the ball and called for the mark, but it came out as he hit the ground. A ball that comes loose on contact with the ground was never controlled, and no control means no mark, so the ball was live and Grandidier-Nkanang, following up his own kick, picked up and scored. Karl Dickson saw it, explained it clearly and got it absolutely spot on. France have had a greater turnover at fly-half this year than most modern governments manage in 10, and the injury list is now endemic. With Ntamack off, Matthieu Jalibert and Thomas Ramos already out and Antoine Hastoy injuring his ankle before the camp began, Galthié simply doesn’t have a specialist 10 of real calibre to call on, and it’s almost certain Maxime Lucu and Dupont will form la charnière against South Africa, with the uncapped Louis Le Brun, the only other option at 10 left in the squad. Lucu does bring a genuinely deep kicking game, but as a nine he’s lateral and doesn’t drive a side forward, and against the Springboks’ line speed that will be a real concern. It’s ironic that the old Hospital-Dieu on the banks of the Rhône is now a beautiful hotel, because on tonight’s evidence Lyon might have needed to reopen it had France picked up any more injuries. Galthié also needs his maul back, because four dropped drives in a half is one thing against Fiji, but against the Springboks it would be fatal. He needs to rebalance that back-row too; whilst Cros was good, Woki had his moments and Boudehent was very physical, Ollivon certainly made the case for his inclusion in his 23 minutes on the pitch, and it might need a rethink of the back five if France are to beat South Africa. Meanwhile, somewhere in Paris, the Springbok squad will be quietly munching biltong, drinking Klippies, FaceTiming their kids, sending each other Instagram messages and half-watching the video of this match, and take it from us, they’ll be worried about absolutely nothing whatsoever. title: 'Completely unfair': Auckland FC coach takes aim after derby draw - NZ Herald
content:
Thunderstorm warning: Alert issued for torrential rain, hail and lightning in Canterbury Auckland FC's Pedro Moreira felt his side deserved a win over the Wellington Phoenix. Photo / Photosport Pedro Moreira believes Auckland FC deserved to win their A-League derby with Wellington Phoenix, insisting the goalless draw was “completely unfair” after a dominant second-half display from the Black Knights. After an even opening 45 minutes, Auckland came out firing after the break, dominating possession and
creating the better opportunities, but they were unable to find the finishing touch, as Logan Rogerson and Sam Cosgrove were among those unable to convert their chances. It was the first time Auckland had failed to beat Wellington in the rivalry, having won previous derby meetings across the opening two seasons. Moreira was encouraged by his side’s performance but disappointed they could not turn their dominance into three points. “I’m happy about the performance, not happy with the result completely because it was completely unfair what happened in the game, especially in the second half, the way that we dominated the game,” Moreira said. “We cannot create such chances like we create and don’t score, so it’s probably what we must really improve in the future.” The match was delayed by an hour before kickoff due to lightning around Go Media Stadium, but Moreira insisted the disruption had no bearing on the contest. “I think it was no difference,” he said. “Since the moment that it starts, I think it was really the same. No change.” While Auckland were left frustrated, Wellington Phoenix coach Chris Greenacre was pleased with the resilience his side showed to withstand the pressure and earn a valuable point. The result sees Phoenix head into the international break top of the A-League table with three wins and a draw from their opening four matches. “I think we’ve got to start somewhere,” Greenacre said. “We haven’t been in front in a derby either, so for us a point away from home is a good point. “I thought we created some big moments in the first half and couldn’t capitalise. Then in the second half they did the same, so I think it could have gone either way and maybe a draw’s a fair result.” Greenacre said the result was important in restoring balance to a rivalry dominated by Auckland. “We had to stop the rot and not allow it to be totally one-sided and, with all due respect to Auckland, it’s been totally one-sided,” he said. “It was really important that we got some credit back and I’d like to think we got some credit back.” For Auckland, the draw leaves them fifth on five points after four matches, but Moreira believes the performance against the league leaders was a significant step forward. Moreira is confident his side is beginning to rediscover their confidence after a difficult period. They started the season with a win over Melbourne City before a thumping loss to the Western Sydney Wanderers was followed by a last-minute draw with Brisbane Roar. “We must start to play without fear sometimes,” he said. “Probably after the defeat in Sydney, we created a few doubts. The boys showed today something different than they showed in the last games and probably it’s because of that.” Attention turns to the next chapter of the rivalry, with Auckland travelling to Wellington for the return derby on December 19. Ben Francis is an Auckland-based reporter for the New Zealand Herald who covers breaking sports news. Neither side could find the back of the net in a match delayed by lightning strikes.

title: Ireland v Argentina: Five takeaways as 'outstanding' Hugo Keenan shines to leave 'harsh truth' for Felipe Contepomi - Planet Rugby
content: Ireland full-back Hugo Keenan celebrates. Hugo Keenan helped himself to a hat-trick as Ireland ran in six tries to beat Argentina 42-12 at the Aviva Stadium, with Los Pumas’ set-piece and defence coming apart after a bright opening quarter. For the first quarter of an hour this resembled a proper Test match, with Argentina looking as though they’d learned something from Shaun Edwards, blitzing hard off the second and third man whilst Marcos Kremer and Juan Martín González knocked Irish carriers backwards. Behind them Tomás Albornoz pulled the strings, and when the Toulon maestro landed a brilliant left-footed cross-kick on Mateo Carreras in the corner on nine minutes, the Pumas’ travelling faithful had every reason to think this might be the night they finally won in Dublin. That was as good as it got. Ireland found a way round every problem Los Pumas set them. Going round the edge of the rush for Keenan‘s first try on 14 minutes started the rout, and from there they turned almost every visit to the Argentine 22 into seven points, wrapping up the bonus point a minute into the second half. The harsh truth for Felipe Contepomi is that most of the damage was self-inflicted. The lineout was an unmitigated disaster, the defence off set-piece was dismal, with a man short at the back and defenders standing off mauls, and a restart that went out on the full was the very definition of a coach-killer. Yellow cards for Justo Piccardo and Efrain Elias then cost 14 points whilst they were in the bin. And here’s the crazy thing: Argentina won more turnovers than Ireland, seven to five, missed one fewer tackle and had 62 per cent of the ball after the break, but Ireland had 70 per cent of the territory in that half, so Los Pumas had plenty of possession and nowhere useful to take it. Keenan was outstanding, carrying for 106 metres and making four clean breaks alongside his three tries, whilst Craig Casey ran the game quietly and sensibly at scrum-half for 54 minutes. After that opening burst, though, Ireland hardly had to get out of third gear, and Argentina have so much more than they showed tonight, which made it an incredibly frustrating evening for them. One of the big talking points going into this Test was Ireland’s half-back selection, with Munster’s Casey preferred to Jamison Gibson-Park and Sam Prendergast retained after coming back into form for Leinster. A word, first, for Casey, who was superb for his 54 minutes. What he did best of all was not overplay his hand; he gave Ireland quick, accurate service, kept clear options open for his backs and brought them into the game time and again. He wasn’t faultless, since Albornoz’s cross-kick went over him on the far side, where the height mismatch with Carreras left him turning to chase, but for control, front-foot rugby and bringing his runners in off his shoulder, Casey made the shirt his own tonight. Ireland v Argentina, AS IT HAPPENED: Coverage of the Nations Championship fixture Prendergast perhaps struggled a tad early doors, standing deep and passing slowly into the teeth of Argentina’s blitz, and both his handling and his kicking were tentative in that first ten minutes. On 14 minutes, though, he made the extra man to get round the edge of the rush, and Robert Baloucoune put a lovely pass inside for Keenan’s first try, and on 41 minutes he went through for a try of his own. Yes, Ireland’s back-row put him in some really good positions to play, but Casey’s control and Prendergast’s moments were more than enough on a night when Argentina simply gave too much away. Key to this impressive Irish victory was the way the hosts adapted to the gaps and opportunities Argentina offered them. In the first half Ireland visited the 22 three times and scored three converted tries, whilst Argentina went in five times and came away with only five points, and that describes the game in one line. Argentina, with a powerful rolling maul and some really strong carrying, had the better of the early exchanges and the collisions, but Ireland took the scoreboard through the sheer efficiency of their red-zone work. It was clear in those opening exchanges that Argentina could dominate the aerial contest, which stood at 6-2 to Los Pumas at the 20-minute mark, and with Prendergast’s early kicking tentative, Ireland, much to their credit, stopped kicking contestables to the Argentine back three. They kept the ball in hand and made Argentina tackle, moving their big men across the pitch to attack the weaker shoulders of smaller defenders such as Albornoz at 10 and Piccardo at 13, and every phase Ireland kept was another set of tackles for a side who hadn’t played a Test since early September and were working under a new defence coach. By 25 minutes the intensity had gone, the system had collapsed and the set piece was creaking. Keenan’s hat-trick deserves its own mention. The first, on 14 minutes, finished the move that took Ireland round the edge of the blitz; on 29 minutes he finished brilliantly after Ireland stole Argentina’s ball on the Pumas’ own five-metre line; and on 49 minutes, after wonderful handling from Joe McCarthy and Ryan Baird in midfield, he ran a beautiful line under the posts to complete the set. It was a really impressive display from the British and Irish Lions full-back, who put Argentina to the sword without ever looking stretched. One of the themes of this window’s build-up has been the noise around Edwards’ move to Argentina, after he said Steve Borthwick had turned down his offer to join England, yet on tonight’s evidence you might conclude that England and Borthwick dodged a bullet, as Argentina’s defence fell apart, in both system and intensity, under Irish pressure. Most worrying of all, the biggest failures came off set-piece, and that’s unforgivable, because set-piece defence is a system thing, the one part of the game a coach can drill during the week. For the first 15 minutes Argentina looked something like an Edwards defence, with a hard blitz from the second and third man out and Bautista Delguy shooting in from 14, which pushed Prendergast deep and slowed Ireland’s passing along the back line. Then Ireland adapted, kicking less and getting big runners into controlled collision channels, and the Pumas’ line stopped staying square; the rushers came in at an angle, space opened up outside them and Ireland went round the edge for Keenan’s first try. Ireland player ratings: ‘Simply brilliant’ hat-trick hero the standout but ‘transformative night’ for Sam Prendergast and some ‘robust’ forwards González and Kremer will have nightmares when they see the replay of Prendergast’s try. González was beaten on the inside shoulder, a cardinal sin at this level, and to compound matters Kremer, the double-team man outside him, grasped at thin air as the Irish 10 went through a hole that simply shouldn’t exist in a Test match. It didn’t stop there. Off lineout ball, Argentina failed to defend a simple long throw to the back and a flip inside, which is a pure system error, and they stood off Ireland’s maul, leaving space down the narrow side for Baloucoune and Keenan to combine. Those things should never happen in elite rugby, and alongside the Pumas’ own lineout failures they show how far the basics of Argentina’s game had deserted them. A lot of that rests at Edwards’ door. He only joined Argentina at the start of this month, so some will say he hasn’t had enough time, but set-piece defence is the one thing you can drill in a week, and that’s exactly where Argentina were found out. Contepomi spent the best years of his career in this city in a Leinster shirt, so a homecoming that ended like this will hurt, and it’s not the margin that will keep him awake tonight. He’ll be thinking about how quickly his side’s structures came apart once Ireland put them under pressure, and how a squad with this much talent showed so little of it. Want more from Planet Rugby? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for world-class coverage you can trust. The fix starts at the lineout, because that’s where the chain began: lose your own throw and the ball goes to Ireland whilst your defence is still getting into shape, and Ireland, who helped themselves to six Pumas throws, punished it almost every time. Next comes the set-piece defence, where one man short at the back, the inside ball and standing off the maul are a week’s work on the training paddock, which is exactly the week Edwards now gets before Genoa. Tidy up the discipline, two yellow cards and a steady stream of penalties, and there’s plenty to build on, because whenever Albornoz, Santiago Chocobares and Carreras had the ball in their hands, Argentina looked capable of hurting anyone. Ireland have the happier week, though not an entirely comfortable one. Prendergast had his moments and Casey was quietly excellent, which leaves Andy Farrell with a call at 10, either sticking with Prendergast for South Africa or giving Ciarán Frawley a start against Fiji. The bigger job is the kicking game. Ireland adapted well tonight by taking it out of the match once they were losing in the air, but that only worked because Argentina kept giving the ball back, and South Africa won’t; against the Springboks you can’t keep the ball in hand for 80 minutes, so Ireland have to compete in the air or they’ll spend long stretches in their own half, in a pressure cooker that has seen off plenty of teams over the years. Fiji are at the Aviva next Saturday with South Africa a week later, whilst Argentina head to Genoa to face Italy before France in Paris. See you after the international break as we host Fulham at the Etihad. “Now it's the international break and in the same way we have done the first one, we’re going to use this international break to try to clarify what we can do better. “We know we can do some things better and we know we need to improve things. “We're going to use that and understand how we can avoid these kinds of games.” “I will speak quite clearly. In the first half when you do not match the intensity and lose all the duels, it is difficult. Then we want to react but it is too late. “In these kinds of matches, first of all you need to match the intensity and win the duels. Otherwise it is always complicated. “In the first half we were not good enough in terms of duels and second balls, we lost all of them. “Then when we tried to react, we were 2-0 down and in football it is always complicated. “The first goal we are trying to play and build up. It can happen. It’s the second one, we lost duels in the middle of the pitch, the third one we lost duels in the edge of the box. “Obviously if you concede two goals against a team like this, away, it’s always difficult to come back because they play then very defensive and wait on the counter attack. “Second-half we reacted well but then they scored and it changed the game. “Obviously the third goal came at the wrong moment. We were in a good moment and then they scored on a counter-attack and we had to start over again. “We didn’t start the game well and then it’s always difficult to come back away against teams like this. We need to do better.” Elliot Anderson thanks the away fans for their support. “Maybe a bit of a rest for those not going away. Mentally more than anything else. “The manager will look back and see a lot of positives and also where we can improve.” “2-0 at half-time. Back into in the second half. It was unbelievable goal from Cherki. “If we’d got the second, you feel we’d go and win the game. “Credit to Liam Delap, it was a sensational finish, it put the game to bed.”

title: ‘The spiritual home of Kiwi rugby’: World reacts to All Blacks’ Murrayfield romp - NZ Herald
content:

How the world’s media reacted to the All Blacks’ 43-21 victory over Scotland at Murrayfield. Scotland never got going; Murrayfield never got going; New Zealand did. Scotland have had some agonising defeats here in recent years, as
they chase that first win against the All Blacks. This was not one of them. This was dispiritingly routine. Despite a hat-trick of tries from Ewan Ashman, the irrepressible hooker, in the first half, Scotland could not register a point in the second. New Zealand cantered away to a tally of seven tries, two for Beauden Barrett, who beetled through Scotland’s outside defences with ease, scoring 19 unanswered points in the second half. We always speculate at this time of year whether it is to the advantage of the southern-hemisphere teams to arrive in the north fully match fit, or whether they might be fatigued at the end of their season. There was no question which team looked on it for this one. Scotland looked disconnected, which might be expected in their first outing of the season, but that hasn’t been the case in those agonising defeats at this same time of year in the past. This flop will prove galling. Whether it will feel so for the north in general, as the devisers of this weird Nations Championship will hope, remains to be seen. There may or may not be much esprit de corps among the teams of the north, but one thing is for sure: the All Blacks and the Springboks look a class apart at the top of the south’s table. Four wins out of four; four bonus points out of four. Two rounds of round-robin to play. At times tries seemed almost too easy to come by. That applied to Scotland as much as the other way round in the first half, when seven tries were scored, but the home team could not rejoin the party after the break. New Zealand’s 121-year win record against Scotland, and now a 21-match unbeaten streak at Murrayfield, remains regally unblemished. Other than Eden Park, the spiritual home of Kiwi rugby, where the All Blacks have not lost in 54 matches, global rugby’s most famous side prefer playing nowhere more than in the Scottish capital. Every time, Scotland question whether it might be their time, but the agonising wait – 34 attempts and counting – continues. A Beauden Barrett double plus a couple of nifty lineout scores prolonged Scottish agony, but the hosts were not hard done by. These All Blacks, on an upward curve under former Glasgow coach Dave Rennie, were a level above the spirited showing Scotland could muster, and the visiting victory was clinical, commanding and convincing. Ewan Ashman, Scotland’s hooker, made history as the first of his countrymen to score a hat-trick against New Zealand – all in the first half, too – but that was somewhat of a red herring. Scotland did manage a couple of maul tries of their own, but across the 80 minutes the hosts were monstered in the tight. The Scottish scrum, in particular, desperately needed emergency repairs; alas, for the capacity home crowd, those never fully materialised. It was an emotional opening November fixture for the All Blacks, too. Earlier this week, it was announced that their head of security, Logan Cadwallader, had died in the team hotel. The visitors could not have done him prouder. Certainly, the axis of Damian McKenzie – despite an off-day with the boot – Jordie Barrett, Quinn Tupaea and Beauden Barrett, in all its poetic fluidity, provided the classiest tribute. After a tough first half against Scotland, the All Blacks stepped up their game after the break, unleashing their running style and securing a comfortable 43-21 victory at Murrayfield. New Zealand have now won all four of their Nations Championship matches. The All Blacks, unbeaten against Scotland for 121 years, were playing for their status at Murrayfield. Trailing the Scots at halftime (21-24), they conceded no points in the second half, during which they inflicted a resounding 19-0 defeat on Gregor Townsend’s men. Full of desire, both in their eagerness to attack swiftly and their ferocious defence, the Scots delivered an admirable first half. They did concede four New Zealand tries, but they fought back through sheer willpower, epitomised by their hooker Ewan Ashman, who scored a hat-trick (7th, 25th, 37th minutes). This allowed them to stay within striking distance at halftime. The pre-match atmosphere had been moving, with national anthems sung in profound silence. The All Blacks wore white jerseys with a black armband on their left arm, over their heart, in tribute to Logan Cadwallader, their head of security for the past 10 years, who died last Sunday in their hotel. Logan was their confidant but also their protector, discreet and effective, who had served in the SAS – the New Zealand Special Forces – and had seen action in Bosnia, East Timor and Afghanistan. The Scottish bagpipes, perched on the roof of Murrayfield Stadium, piercing the silence, had a special ring to them. Ruthless New Zealand blew Scotland away in a high-class, seven tries to three Nations Championship victory at Murrayfield. Despite a historic first-half hat-trick from Scotland hooker Ewan Ashman, the All Blacks were mostly magnificent, unrelenting and classy. It was the 34th test between the nations and New Zealand’s tally has yet another win – 32 now, with two draws going back to 1905. Wallace Sititi scored early in a breathless first half. Ashman responded. Ethan de Groot and Codie Taylor hit back to make it 17-7 at the end of the first quarter. New Zealand’s Peter Lakai was binned and Ashman got his second while he was off. The sensational Beauden Barrett scored the first of his double straight after. Then, as the bonkerdom stretched on, Sititi was yellow-carded, and Ashman made the All Blacks pay with his hat-trick try. Only three points divided them at the break, but the All Blacks outclassed Scotland thereafter. Josh Moorby, Beauden Barrett again and Asafo Aumua struck in the second half. Scotland were beaten out the gate in the end. We hoped for a classic and a classic it was, with bells on. If only for 40 minutes. Beyond that thrilling opening spell it was one-way traffic, a vicious exhibition of All Black class and might. Ewan Ashman became only the fifth player to score a hat-trick against New Zealand, but it was not enough to prevent Scotland going down to yet another defeat in this fixture. The Scots sensed an opportunity to end their long wait for a first victory over the All Blacks after Edinburgh hooker Ashman notched a treble to keep them within three points of their visitors at the end of an epic, seven-try first half. But the hosts lost their way after the break as Dave Rennie’s on-song side closed out an ultimately comfortable 43-21 Nations Championship triumph. Scotland, who were given something of a reality check as they were unable to score a point in the second half, have now failed to defeat New Zealand in 34 meetings since they first locked horns in 1905. There was a moment’s applause ahead of kickoff in memory of former Edinburgh captain Ally Donaldson, who died in September, and long-serving All Blacks head of security Logan Cadwallader, who died in Edinburgh last weekend. The sun peeked through Edinburgh clouds long enough just before kickoff at Murrayfield to offer a ray of hope that this could be Scotland’s breakthrough day against the All Blacks. For a fleeting time in the first half, while the All Blacks conceded two yellow cards, Scotland closed within range and dared to dream. Come the second half, though, normal service resumed as the free-wheeling All Blacks turned to their scrum platform to reassert their dominance and extend their 121-year, 34-test unbeaten record against Scotland with a 43-21 win. In an emotional occasion, the All Blacks paid tribute to Logan Cadwallader, their head of security and former Special Airforce Soldier who died suddenly in Edinburgh last Sunday, by wearing black armbands and etching his initials and military number into their white shirt. Cadwallader’s brother and son, Trey, linked arm-and-arm with captain Codie Taylor as the All Blacks sang the New Zealand anthem – and the bench then joined in performing the Ka Mate haka from the sideline. In an entertaining, eventful match between two teams with similar attacking ambition, the All Blacks honoured Cadwallader by securing a result befitting his service. The All Blacks were far from perfect. Their ball skills weren’t always slick. Discipline will be a major focus for improvement, and defensively they were exposed at times, but they summoned composure to ride through that adversity and emerge with a bonus-point victory that maintains their quest for the inaugural Nations Championship final. ANALYSIS: The win in Scotland saw the All Blacks take another step forward.

Showed intent to put pressure on Scotland at the breakdown at the ruck to create a turnover early on, though he was shown a yellow card in the first half for perhaps being a touch too eager in that area. Assisted on both Beauden Barrett tries and beat a few defenders. Another outing that makes you believe McKenzie could yet be a long-term option in the No 10 jersey. Limited impact but took his opportunity to get on the scoreboard when it was presented and showed great hustle to get in position to hold up Scotland centre Huw Jones over the line. Forced off late for a head injury assessment after running into Blair Kinghorn’s shoulder. Took plenty of carries, secured a turnover and had a lovely looping pass to assist on Moorby’s try, but missed a few tackles and perhaps didn’t quite have the same sort of impact we’ve become accustomed to from him. Had the novelty of packing down on the side of the scrum when the All Blacks were down to 13 at one point. He was ultimately named the official man of the match. Did some good cleanout work and while he gave away a scrum penalty soon after entering the contest, he was strong in that area as the game went on. Entered the contest for an 18-minute cameo and didn’t put a foot wrong. Had limited opportunities to make his mark, entering the game with just nine minutes left on the clock. Returned from injury for a 24-minute outing off the bench and picked up right where he left off, bringing physicality on both ends of the floor. A sure-handed presence in the final 20 minutes, moving the ball along nicely and kicking well. Entered the contest with 15 minutes to play but didn’t get many opportunities to show if he can be that attacking spark off the bench many expect from him. Injected into the game with about 30 minutes remaining as Jordan appeared to be carrying a niggle. He broke the line once but had to fight to make an impact. title: Holden's fingerprints are still on Cadillac's V8 CT5-V Blackwing, says engineer - CarExpert
content: We use cookies to give you the best possible experience on the CarExpert website, to analyse our traffic and make sure that any advertising that is delivered is personalised to you. To find out more, visit our privacy policy. The rear-drive platform under Cadillac's fire-breathing V8 sedan was a joint effort with Holden - and its suspension geometry has barely changed since. Holden may have stopped building cars in Australia almost a decade ago, but a piece of it lives on in one of the best performance sedans you can buy in the US. Speaking to CarExpert at a recent General Motors event in New York, Cadillac vehicle performance engineer Tom Schinderle said the Alpha rear-wheel drive platform underpinning Cadillac's sedans was developed alongside Holden. "The Alpha chassis itself, right? That was a true collaboration effort between Holden and North America, and that set the basis for the following generation, and then where we are today," Schinderle said. CarExpert can help you research, compare and buy so you choose with confidence. Today's Cadillac CT5-V Blackwing rides on an evolution of that architecture, and according to Mr Schinderle, the bones are much the same as they were when it first launched. "We've made a lot of suspension changes from a tuning standpoint, but the overall geometry is very similar to what it was back then. We've made tweaks here and there, and I'm continuing to make tweaks as we're working on the car," he said. A good example is the Precision Package, offered on the facelifted CT5-V Blackwing. It brings stiffer springs and anti-roll bars, revised bushings, new steering knuckles and rear toe links, carbon-ceramic brakes, and Michelin Pilot Sport Cup 2 R tyres. "It's got different bushings, different stabiliser bars, different springs, but the geometry is mostly the same," Schinderle said. "We're able to just continue to make the car slightly better, slightly better every time we touch it." Mr Schinderle said the Holden-era collaboration was slightly before his time. He started out in structure and chassis design and release engineering before moving to performance, by which point GM was more focused on North American product. But the Australian link to Alpha ran deeper than many realise. Holden's powertrain calibration team was spotted testing a Cadillac ATS-V – another Alpha car – on Australian roads in 2016, and even after local manufacturing ended the team continued work. HSV also sold a right-hand drive conversion of the Alpha-based sixth-generation Chevrolet Camaro here, which ended up being the only vehicle offered here on this platform. While lesser CT5s use turbocharged four-cylinder and twin-turbo V6 engines, the flagship CT5-V Blackwing is the closest thing on sale today to the last of the great Commodores. It's the same formula: a big V8 up front, drive to the rear wheels, and enough comfort to use every day. In this case, it's a supercharged 6.2-litre V8 with 498kW (668hp) and 893Nm, paired with a six-speed manual or 10-speed automatic. The last Australian-built Commodore rolled off the line at Elizabeth in October 2017. If you were a fan of the final SS-V Redline, you'd love the CT5-V Blackwing – it has character for days, sounds incredible, and really sings when you push it. Unfortunately, it's not coming here. The CT5-V Blackwing is built in left-hand drive only, and Cadillac's Australian lineup is entirely electric. That's a real shame, because it would have found a ready-made audience in this country – one that, in a roundabout way, helped create it. While GM has previously confirmed the current-generation CT5 range will end production this year, it has announced a new generation is coming. GM Authority reports it'll use an updated version of the outgoing model's existing platform and enter production in the second half of 2028. title: Nottingham Forest 3-1 Man City: How the players rated - BBC
content: Delap brace inspires Forest to stunning win over Man City Liam Delap scored twice against his old club to help Nottingham Forest to victory and inflict a third straight Premier League loss on Manchester City. Here's how I rated the players and and you can see how you scored them below. Matz Sels: Could do nothing about Rayan Cherki's goal. 6 Daniel Munoz: Looked pumped and did superbly to keep the dangerous Jeremy Doku quiet. 7 Jair Cunha: The centre-back found himself in attack in the sixth minute, when he pounced before coolly rolling in the opener. Made a brilliant goalline clearance at the other end. 8 Nikola Milenkovic: Stood tall to block a Jeremy Doku strike early on which epitomised his overall showing. 7 Murillo: The Brazilian was solid and did what was asked of him, to help stop Erling Haaland. 7 Neco Williams: Got stuck in when required. A solid performance. 7 Ryan Yates: The captain's poor clearance allowed Cherki to score in the second half. 6 Xaver Schlager: Provided the assist for the second goal in a decent showing. 7 James McAtee: Had a very good game against his former club. Could have enjoyed a goal but had a weak shot saved, before blazing another over. 7 Morgan Gibbs-White: Hard-working and caused City a few problems in the final third. 7 Liam Delap: A double for the no-nonsense ex-City striker. Two thunderous finishes brought the stadium alive. 9 Subs not used: John Victor, Ousmane Diomande, Callum Hudson-Odoi, Chris Wood, Arnaud Kalimuendo. Gianluigi Donnarumma: Another game without a clean sheet, another three conceded. Aerially suspect too. Not having a good season. 4 Abdukodir Khusanov: Seems awkward when shunted out to the right, before being moved back inside. 4 Ruben Dias: A desperate lunge to try to block Delap's goal summed up his - and his side's - poor display. 4 Marc Guehi: Part of a City defence that were all over the place in the first half before being hooked at half-time. 4 Josko Gvardiol: Not in great form at the moment. Soft on the ball early on when he had his pocket picked by Cunha for Forest's opener and was also substituted. 4 Elliot Anderson: Made an unhappy return to the City Ground where he lost the midfield battle. 5 Enzo Fernandez: A really disappointing performance. Should have pulled a goal back but sent his header from close range over. Midfield seems to lack in balance with him and Anderson in the side. 5 Jeremy Doku: Got no change out of Munoz and produced very little. 5 Iliman Ndiaye: Missed interception led to Forest's second goal and did not contribute much in attack. Not his best game. 5 Rayan Cherki: Pulled a goal back for City with a stunning finish in the second half. 6 Erling Haaland: Had some chances but not his best showing in front of goal. 5 Matheus Nunes (on 45, Guehi) Failed to put a foot in on Delap for Forest's third. 5 Nico O'Reilly (on 45, Gvardiol) With Gvardiol shaky, will the Englishman be given a run of games in the side? 6 Subs not used: Geronimo Rulli, Mateo Kovacic, Vitor Reis, Ayyoub Bouaddi, Allan, Rico Lewis. title: Wales v Japan: Five takeaways as Eddie Jones' men will be 'fuming' as Steve Tandy's charges survive an 'unmitigated disaster' - Planet Rugby
content: Wales winger Josh Adams and an inset of Japan captain Warner Dearns. Following Wales’ 28-21 victory over Japan in the Nations Championship clash at the Principality Stadium in Cardiff, here are our five takeaways. It’s heartbreak for Japan again as Wales held on to beat the Brave Blossoms with Josh Adams scoring twice and winning the decisive turnover at the death in a game the visitors dominated at the set piece and breakdown but couldn’t finish. Eddie Jones said the first 20 minutes would be pretty important and wanted a hot start for his side, but unfortunately for the Japan coach he got a rather cold one, as prop Archie Griffin smashed over after three minutes. The move started with a brilliant run from player of the match Louis Rees-Zammit, then came a Japanese offside, a kick to the corner and a lineout play out the back door that caught the visitors’ maul defenders slow to get up and around. It couldn’t have been less hot for the visitors. But what followed was a really great Test match, and both sides deserve credit for the ball-in-play time and the ambition, but, worryingly for Steve Tandy, it was one Japan controlled for long stretches, carrying 82 times toe credit for the ball-in-play Wales’ 54, with 61 per cent of the ball after the break and Wales tackling 235 times to the visitors’ 122. Unfortunately for Japan, they never quite managed to throw the knockout punch. Looking back across the evidence and the key is that Wales won the big moments; it was as simple as that. Nicky Smith won a turnover on his own line right on half-time when Japan looked set to draw level, and Dewi Lake and Rhys Carré did exactly the same at critical moments after the break. When Japan got narrow in attack and lost the ball in contact, Blair Murray collected and Adams went 80 metres for his second try, and he followed that up with the final turnover from Japan’s last scrum, with the Brave Blossoms camped in the Welsh half needing a converted try for the draw. The result flatters Wales and probably doesn’t do Japan justice, but the Blossoms were the masters of their own downfall. A year on from losing 24-23 here, when Jarrod Evans kicked the winner after the hooter and a lineout penalty that looked clear and obvious went unawarded, they’ll be fuming at letting another one slip, even with a losing bonus point to take away. Harry Hockings, whose late card in that game was later rescinded, carried 18 times today, more than anyone on the pitch, and both he and Warner Dearns were outstanding in the engine room. For long stretches the visitors were superb. Their rugby was outstanding, with Naoto Saito running the game with real authority, his time at Toulouse having sharpened his game beyond belief, and the quick ball he and the Japanese breakdown created put the Welsh defence around the ruck under real pressure in the first half, with the guards and pillars never quite set in time. Their back-row was brilliant. Ben Gunter scored the first try on ten minutes, after Murray took a fine catch but didn’t call a mark and Wales left the ball exposed at the bottom of the ruck, and he then drove off a lineout, taking two Welsh defenders with him, for Dearns’ try. It was a switch-pod move that shifted the point of contact so well that Wales were looking at each other in despair as the big man clattered over, and it had Jones and Neal Hatley written all over it. As the game went on, Dearns and Jack Cornelsen took the Welsh lineout apart, holding Wales to 69 per cent on their own throw whilst winning every one of Japan’s; if lineouts were cakes, Dearns would be walking off this pitch a stone heavier tonight. Kippei Ishida’s footwork was reminiscent of Shane Williams, which is quite a thing to say in Cardiff, with Samisoni Tua (16 carries) and Dylan Riley giving him great support in midfield, Kazuma Ueda beating nine defenders from full-back and Cornelsen carrying 15 times on top of his lineout work. The bench had a real say too, Kenta Fukuda flying over on 75 minutes after replacement hooker Kenji Sato, standing on the wing, stepped Adams and offloaded. Whilst Japan were accurate at times, they were short of confidence at others, and it showed in the last five metres. Too often they kicked the ball away at the end of promising attacking moves, twice in the second half they were held up or turned over five metres out, and that final ruck before the line kept eluding them. They’ll grow from this. Italy v Springboks: Five takeaways as ‘ice-cold’ South Africa floor Azzurri but why Rassie Erasmus won’t be happy ahead of French ‘grudge match’ Wales’ strength was their first-phase carry. When Rees-Zammit, Max Llewellyn and Eddie James got over the gainline off set piece, their backs had a clear picture of where to attack, and Wales made 471 metres from 54 carries, an outstanding 8.7 metres a carry against Japan’s 4.8, with Rees-Zammit alone beating 14 defenders. He looks a different player now, bigger and more muscular, and he finished a beauty on 37 minutes after James had smashed it up into contact, taken out Japan’s folding defence on the right and sat the cover down. James was powerful in contact all afternoon, and at 104kg against Saito’s 75kg we saw one of the collisions of the season as he flattened the scrum-half in attack. What Tandy will be pleased about is that Wales are building a core of good players and leaders, with Carré, Lake, Jac Morgan, Rees-Zammit and Tomos Williams all very good. Williams threw 64 passes and had two try assists, Murray beat ten defenders from full-back, and the tight five tackled themselves to a standstill, Dafydd Jenkins making 25 and Morgan 24. Carré and Ryan Elias made a real impact off the bench, and Dan Edwards came on to convert Adams’ second after a lacklustre display from Sam Costelow before he made way for Edwards. All Blacks player ratings v Scotland: Beauden Barrett’s ‘renaissance’ continues while scrum shines in fine all-round display When he looks back at this, Tandy will admit the lineout was an unmitigated disaster, as his charges lost seven throws to Japan’s jumpers thus handing the visitors possession they simply didn’t have to earn. Then there’s the attacking shape, where the centres’ alignment and spacing were terrible at times and there was no looping fly-half coming round after the first receiver to connect the attack; Wales kept going cross-field with numbers, eating up their own space before the ball could reach the overlap and making it easy for Japan’s wide defence to pick them off. Want more from Planet Rugby? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for world-class coverage you can trust. The Welsh work around the ruck in the first half was downright awful at times too, and that’s where Japan’s tempo hurt them most, although it tightened up after the break and stayed good and legal once Japan started throwing the kitchen sink at them. The penalty count will also concern Tandy, and Wales let Japan straight back in after scoring on three occasions, Gunter crossing seven minutes after Griffin’s opener, Dearns four minutes after Adams’ first and Fukuda seven minutes after Adams’ second. You can be absolutely sure New Zealand won’t let them off like that. Scotland v New Zealand: Five takeaways as All Blacks pass litmus test with ‘flying colours’ despite benefitting from ‘clear and obvious’ obsession Firstly, a word for Riku Kitahara on his debut, with Ryunosuke Ito away on university commitments. The young 10 certainly has fast feet, defended well at times, looked composed early and is certainly promising, but his exits and key decisions gave the ball back to Wales too often, and he kicked aimlessly to their back three, which is the one thing you don’t do against Rees-Zammit, Adams and Murray. Adams’ first try came straight from one of those kicks, and that’s a lesson he’ll need to take on board. Japan also carried into contact far too high in critical moments, which isn’t like them at all given how much work Jones does on body height, and as a result they were ripped four times in the first quarter alone. Their tackling needs work too; they missed 41 tackles to Wales’ 23, a 67 per cent success rate, and that’s how the Welsh back three were allowed to do their damage. It’s also worth remembering how much Japan are missing, with Ito and Michael Leitch absent, and Jones, who said in the summer that around ten players who’d normally be in his top 23 were unavailable, has been rebuilding around absentees all year, which makes the performance all the more encouraging. That won’t ease the pain of another narrow loss in Cardiff, though, a place where Jones is desperate to win. title: Scotland v All Blacks: Winners and losers as Dave Rennie 'clearly turns the tide' while it's the same old story for Gregor Townsend - Planet Rugby
content: All Blacks back Beauden Barrett and an inset of Scotland's Blair Kinghorn. Following the All Blacks’ 43-21 victory over Scotland, we pick out our winners and losers from the action at Murrayfield Stadium in the Nations Championship. The All Blacks came into this match off the back of successive victories over the Wallabies in the Bledisloe Cup but a hat-trick of defeats to the Springboks in Rugby’s Greatest Rivalry series. That meant that new head coach Dave Rennie boasted a record of six wins from nine Tests, hardly a marvellous record for what the job demands. However, pressure wasn’t mounting, with pundits and the New Zealand public well aware that serious shifts needed to be made for next year’s Rugby World Cup following Scott Robertson’s tenure in charge. The performance of the All Blacks at Murrayfield on Saturday perhaps showed precisely why New Zealand Rugby made the decision that they did, as it was far from the great Damian McKenzie escape that we witnessed 12 months ago at this venue. Instead, it was a polished, accurate and well-coached team that kept a strong Scottish outfit pointless in the second half and ruthlessly made the most of their opportunities. Rennie has a 70% Test win record now, and the big caveat is that he has overseen four Tests against the top-ranked team in the world, three of which took place on South African shores. The former Chiefs and Wallabies boss has clearly turned the tide and made the All Blacks into a serious force in international rugby again, and not one that teams fancy creating a bit of history as they did when Robertson was at the helm. My colleague has described Beauden Barrett’s form as a late-career renaissance, and it’s hard to argue against that as the former two-time World Rugby Player of the Year has been nothing short of brilliant in his last three Test appearances. The eldest Barrett brother lacks the pace that he possessed during the earlier knockings of his career, but that is a fair trade-off for the game smarts and tactical brilliance he has garnered over 148 Test matches. He equalled Richie McCaw’s Test cap tally against the Scots on Saturday and created his own bit of history, surpassing Doug Howlett’s try-scoring tally. To add the cherry on top, he grabbed another to bring up his half-century of tries in international rugby. There were those who believed that this year would be the start of Barrett’s stark decline after he fell down the pecking order for New Zealand but the injuries to Ruben Love and Richie Mo’unga have given him the opportunity in the team and he is making the most of it. It wasn’t just that Barrett scored two tries for New Zealand but also his overall performance; he was strong under the high ball, excellent with ball in hand, and was once again a fantastic playmaking partner for Damian McKenzie. While McCaw was 148 and out, evidence suggests that Barrett will reach the 150 mark and beyond. All Blacks player ratings v Scotland: Beauden Barrett’s ‘renaissance’ continues while scrum shines in fine all-round display When Andrew Brace blasted the whistle for the first time at Murrayfield on Saturday, only four men had scored hat-tricks in a Test match against New Zealand, but by half-time, there were five. Ewan Ashman will have wanted to be a part of the first Scotland team to beat New Zealand but can soothe his wounds with the achievement of becoming just the second forward and fifth player to ever cross the All Blacks’ tryline on three occasions in one Test match, following in the footsteps of Australia’s Greg Cornelsen, South Africa’s Ray Mordt and Marius Joubert, as well as Wales’ Tom Rogers. Sure, two of those tries came off the back of driving mauls, but he still had to find his jumper before that could occur, and it matters not how the five-pointers were scored, just that they were. The three tries may also take away some of the shine from his overall individual performance because he was excellent. In fact, one of Scotland’s best even when removing the 15 points. Scotland player ratings v All Blacks: ‘Memorable day’ in defeat for Ewan Ashman while duo can ‘hold heads high’ The glue-man in the All Blacks backline whose work rate, contributions and overall excellence are often outshone by his midfield partner Jordie Barrett. Make no mistake, the youngest Barrett was superb at Murrayfield and was a serious contender for the man of the match award, but frankly, Quinn Tupaea was truly deserving. Players will often shy away from the spotlight of the individual awards but perhaps this is one that Tupaea should embrace more as he continues to make up for lost time at the highest level after that horrid injury that kept him sidelined for so long. Mike Blair and Rennie have been lauded for their work time and time again this year but the spotlight hasn’t quite been shone on the remainder of the coaching ticket but they richly deserved it after the performance in the Scottish capital. Let’s start with Jason Ryan, who has been in the spotlight for all the wrong reasons, with many questioning his ability to turn the All Blacks scrum into a force in the international game again. He achieved that when he first joined the Test team’s set-up under Ian Foster but the scrum in particular fell off a cliff. Small improvements have been made in recent months, and it all came together against Scotland with the men in black properly bossing the set-piece. Ryan’s expertise extends to the lineout too where he has been working alongside the straight-talking Neil Barnes and that is a facet of New Zealand’s game that was put under the cosh by the Springboks and has enjoyed an upward trajectory since. The lineout and scrum were the platforms that the All Blacks were able to strike from and were crucial in the victory. Finally, legendary centre Tana Umaga deserves a doff of the cap after his defence shut out one of the best attacking structures in international rugby for 40 minutes. In fact, only once was his defence breached through open play with two of Scotland’s three tries coming from driving mauls. That is some going in the current game as attack is currently getting the better of defence at the highest level. Scotland v New Zealand: Five takeaways as All Blacks pass litmus test with ‘flying colours’ despite benefitting from ‘clear and obvious’ obsession Given the nod over Pierre Schoeman in the starting line-up against the All Blacks, Rory Sutherland was unable to repay the coaching team’s faith in him and was subsequently hooked before half-time. He battled in the scrums and offered little around the park, with Schoeman making a notable difference in the loose despite having his own struggles in the set-pieces. As mentioned above, the All Blacks needed McKenzie to save the day last year when these two nations met last November, which only gave the Murrayfield faithful more hope that this might just be Scotland’s year. The performances of Glasgow Warriors and Edinburgh in the United Rugby Championship only intensified that hope, but as all sports fans know, it’s the hope that kills you, and Saturday that fact rang true again. The 2025 meeting was close; the 2026 one was too, but only for 40 minutes, and much like the hope killing you, the Scots again were the nearly men, providing the promise that they are different and could get the result that the fans so desperately want but like 2025, this year, Scotland have failed to win the Six Nations and failed to beat the All Blacks. Want more from Planet Rugby? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for world-class coverage you can trust. And that again raises the question that rears its head time and time again… Has Gregor Townsend taken this team as far as he possibly can? It the one raised earlier this year before the Six Nations and after the defeat to Italy, but silenced with wins over England and France. Therein lies the issue. Scotland are more than capable of memorable victories over top teams but are not producing them often enough for what this golden generation deserves. Third place in the World Rugby rankings was a possibility for Scotland in victory, which would have been their highest-ever ranking, but again, the team wasn’t able to rise to the occasion and deliver. There were calls not to extend Townsend’s contract through to the World Cup with Franco Smith taking over after this year’s Six Nations and perhaps the Scottish Rugby Union will live to regret that they didn’t make the decision then, or maybe not. Only time will tell. Injury has kept Richie Mo’unga out of the All Blacks team following Rugby’s Greatest Rivalry series and Rennie has stated that he is likely to return in time for the clash against England with Wales probably a week too soon. However, the axis of McKenzie and Barrett are looking increasingly more difficult to break up with every passing Test match. The duo were outstanding at Eden Park, even better in Sydney and arguably produced their best in the Scottish capital. That will put Rennie and his staff in a difficult position when it comes to nailing down their team for the all-important final match of the Nations Championship regular season match at Twickenham, especially if the Springboks are unbeaten in the competition by that stage too. content: Ewan Ashman scored three tries for Scotland. Following a 43-21 win for New Zealand over Scotland at Murrayfield on Saturday, here’s our player ratings for Gregor Townsend’s men. 15 Kyle Rowe: Nailed a wonderful 50/22 early in the contest which led to Ewan Ashman’s first pushover crossing on seven minutes. Outside of that he ran smart lines that resulted in 50 metres from five carries. Replaced with just 51 minutes on the clock by Blair Kinghorn. 6 14 Kyle Steyn: Didn’t see a great deal of ball on the wing but when Steyn did get his hands on it he was solid in the carry. 5 13 Huw Jones: Wonderful to see him back in a Scotland shirt as there are few better sights than Jones breaking the line at full steam. He fed off Finn Russell’s perfectly weighted passes for a short spell of the game but then New Zealand dominated, which reduced his impact. 6 12 Sione Tuipulotu (c): Led from the front in terms of his carries but unfortunately had to take a yellow card for the team after an offside, this after Scotland’s offences had racked up in the second half. 13 carries from the centre on the day but they weren’t for big metres. 6 11 Jamie Dobie: Toiled away both out wide and coming off his wing as the diminutive back never took a backward step on Saturday. Was up against Will Jordan and he was by no means overawed and probably edged the All Blacks try-scoring great in his individual battle. 7 Scotland v New Zealand: Five takeaways as All Blacks pass litmus test with ‘flying colours’ despite benefitting from ‘clear and obvious’ obsession 10 Finn Russell: Grew into today’s match with those customary floated passes getting the most out of Jones. However, that was as good as it got for Russell who was replaced early in the second half with Townsend seemingly not happy with the way Scotland were tracking. 5 9 Ben White: A steely hit on Jordan set the tone from White before his crisp pass for Ashman’s second try showed his class with ball in hand. Replaced on the hour mark as Scotland looked to find something different, but little changed in what was a scoreless second half. 6 8 Jack Dempsey: Produced some heroic defence to hold up Jordan over the whitewash on 12 minutes. The number eight backed that up with seven barnstorming carries in the Test that saw him end with 42 metres to his name. A decent showing from the burly forward. 6 7 Rory Darge: Didn’t stop all day. The Glasgow Warriors openside emptied the tank for the cause on both sides of the ball, running support lines as well as racking up 22 tackles. Definitely one of a few Scotland players who can hold his head up high after this home defeat. 8 6 Matt Fagerson: Was a carrying threat in the first 40 but didn’t have the same impact in the second before being replaced by Bath’s Josh Bayliss. 5 All Blacks player ratings v Scotland: Beauden Barrett’s ‘renaissance’ continues while scrum shines in fine all-round display 5 Scott Cummings: 14 tackles on the day is a good return but was quiet with the ball while New Zealand turned the screw at both set-pieces. 5 4 Gregor Brown: Hugely impressive in open play as the lock caught the eye at Murrayfield. Brown also chipped in with a brilliant breakdown penalty to relieve the pressure on his team’s 22 just before the break. 16 tackles is solid but a game high 15 carries is immense. 8 Want more from Planet Rugby? Carried pretty well with ball in hand when he got the chance but it’s difficult to ignore the scrum issues. 4 2 Ewan Ashman: Talk about a dream half for Edinburgh’s sole representative in the XV. Three tries to his name, the first and third from the maul while the second came after he hit a superb line off White from five metres out. Not the result but a memorable day for him. 8 1 Rory Sutherland: Appeared to carry the can for a struggling scrum when he was replaced on 32 minutes, with Scotland looking to change the picture in the referee’s mind. In touch at half-time down 21-24 after two All Blacks sin-binnings, Scotland couldn’t add to their score; frustrated by a string of penalties, they conceded 13 to eight and were unable to penetrate a dogged All Blacks defence. A key turnover by centre Quinn Tupaea, a constant threat in the midfield, regained momentum midway through the second half, when the game was meandering, to extend the All Blacks’ lead. Fullback Beauden Barrett benefited from the All Blacks’ attacking approach with two tries, including his 50th in Tests, but the pack's power took the sting out of Scotland. Lock Fabian Holland dominated the lineouts, supported by flanker Tupou Vaa’i, while the front row were controlled and consistent. That was evident when the first scrum of the game came in the 33rd minute, as the All Blacks, with only seven in the scrum, relieved pressure on their line. Then six minutes into the second half, off their own feed, their power earned a penalty out from Scotland’s line. While they didn’t score on the first chance, another Scottish infringement, this time in front of the posts, allowed halfback Cam Roigard to throw a long pass to second five-eighths Jordie Barrett, who threw another long ball to the unmarked left wing Josh Moorby, who scored. Three minutes later, after 51 minutes, Scotland captain Sione Tuipulotu was yellow-carded. The All Blacks took immediate toll, kicking for a lineout and winning the ball with Tupaea playing as stand-off to feed first five-eighths Damian McKenzie, who linked with Beauden Barrett to join the line for his second try of the game, his 50th, to take a 36-21 lead. Barrett pulled off a big defensive play in the 56th minute to break an 18-phase Scotland build-up and deny wing Kyle Steyn a potential try. The play lost momentum, but once Tupaea pulled off a superb tackle and won a turnover penalty, the All Blacks used their lineout to regain it. Vaa’i took the ball deep in the line and fed Lakai on the blindside, where replacement hooker Asafo Aumua ran unchallenged to score. Seven tries told the story of the action-packed first half, four of them to the All Blacks. Flanker Wallace Sititi scored after three minutes from a clever dummy lineout move, and prop Ethan de Groot (15 minutes) crossed off a tap penalty by halfback Cam Roigard just out from the line. That was followed by captain and hooker Codie Taylor (19 mins) crossing from a lineout drive. They lost Lakai to the sin-bin after the All Blacks conceded five consecutive penalties. But the All Blacks countered after a lineout penalty gave McKenzie the chance to throw a long pass to Beauden Barrett (30 mins), who raced into a gap to score. Scotland utilised their lineout drive for hooker Ewan Ashman to score two of his hat-trick of tries (seven and 37 minutes). He was required to run a little further for his third after Scotland ran the ball to the midfield where he made use of a gap created after Sititi’s 32nd minute yellow card. Scotland took the All Blacks on with their backlines, several times creating openings and forcing defensive penalties, while Moorby denied them a try by getting his hands under the ball in a goal-line tackle. The Scots were forced to make 143 tackles compared to 132, while they were unable to make the most of a breakdown advantage of 109-86. The All Blacks denied Scots dangerman first five-eighths Finn Russell to have an influence and that told in the final outcome. Scotland 21 ( Ewan Ashman 3 tries; Finn Russell 3 con) New Zealand 43 (Wallace Sititi, Ethan de Groot, Codie Taylor, Beauden Barrett 2, Josh Moorby, Asafo Aumua tries;  Damian McKenzie 4 con). HT: 21-24

title: All Blacks player ratings v Scotland: Beauden Barrett's 'renaissance' continues while scrum shines in fine all-round display - Planet Rugby
content: Josh Moorby, Beauden Barrett and Ethan De Groot all impressed for the All Blacks against Scotland. After their 43-21 victory over Scotland in their Nations Championship clash at Murrayfield, here’s how the All Blacks team performed on Saturday. 15 Beauden Barrett: The veteran All Blacks utility back has revived his Test career recently, and his renaissance continued in this match as he kept Scotland’s defenders on their toes throughout. Barrett‘s attacking efforts were rewarded with two tries, which brought up a half-century of five-pointers for the All Blacks at Test level and he was solid under the high ball. 8 14 Will Jordan: Although New Zealand’s try-scoring machine did not cross the whitewash in this clash, he asked plenty of questions of Scotland‘s defence and finished with a team-high 59 metres gained. 7 13 Quinn Tupaea: The Chiefs midfielder impressed with his distribution skills in the outside channels but made his biggest contribution on defence where he made 12 tackles and won a crucial turnover. 8 12 Jordie Barrett: The youngest of the Barrett brothers has been in fine form throughout 2026 and this clash was no different as he put in a superb all-round performance. Was brilliant on either side of the ball before being forced off after 65 minutes following a head clash with Blair Kinghorn. 8 11 Josh Moorby: The Hurricanes flyer looked dangerous with ball in hand and crossed for a try early in the second half while he also did well in the aerial duels. 7 10 Damian McKenzie: The diminutive playmaker was shifted to fly-half from full-back with great success against the Wallabies and that continued against Scotland where his playmaking skills created several try-scoring opportunities for his team-mates. Missed some shots at goal off the kicking tee, though. 7 9 Cam Roigard: Continued with his outstanding form as he provided a slick service to his outside backs while also proving to be an attacking threat around the fringes. Replaced by Cortez Ratima on the hour-mark. 7 Scotland v New Zealand: Five takeaways as All Blacks pass litmus test with ‘flying colours’ despite benefitting from ‘clear and obvious’ obsession 8 Wallace Sititi: The 24-year-old was in the thick of the action from the outset and was rewarded with a well-taken try after four minutes and continued to shine on attack as the match progressed. Also spent some time in the sin bin for straying offside on defence late in the second half, but Sititi can be happy with his efforts as he finished with 50 metres gained. 7 7 Peter Lakai: Like his back-row partner Sititi, Lakai was also yellow-carded for a cynical defensive indiscretion after 23 minutes but apart from that, he got through plenty of work on either side of the ball and also crossed the whitewash. 7 6 Tupou Vaa’i: Was on the field for 71 minutes before being replaced by Christian Lio-Willie but Vaa’i proved a handy option at the back of the lineout during his time on the field, while he also put his body on the line on defence. Also got through plenty of work on defence where he made 16 hits. 7 5 Fabian Holland: The All Blacks’ Dutch-born enforcer did what was expected of him at the coalface of their forward effort as he won his fair share of lineout balls and was superb on defence where he made 17 tackles. 7 4 Scott Barrett: Although the former All Blacks skipper was anonymous on attack, he made up for that with a huge defensive effort as he finished with a team-high 21 tackle execution and he also won a couple of turnovers. 8 3 Fletcher Newell: The All Blacks held the upper hand at scrum time as they won some penalties at the set-piece and Newell will be happy with his efforts in that department as he won his direct duel against Rory Sutherland. Eventually replaced by Pasilio Tosi after 63 minutes. 8 2 Codie Taylor (c): Another solid performance from the experienced hooker who impressed as a ball carrier, where he was rewarded with a five-pointer for his efforts, while also shining on defence where he made 14 tackles. Replaced by Asafo Aumua in the 56th minute. 7 1 Ethan de Groot: Like Newell, the burly loosehead prop will be delighted with his scrummaging efforts as he was excellent in the set-piece but also impressed at close quarters on attack and scored a deserved try early in the second half. George Bower replaced him after 50 minutes. 8 Replacements: This match was in the balance at half-time with the All Blacks holding a slender 24-21 lead but their head coach Dave Rennie used his replacements intelligently after the interval. Bower, Tosi and Aumua continued with the excellent scrummaging when coming on in the second half and the latter added the final nail in Scotland’s coffin when he scored New Zealand’s seventh try in the 68th minute. 8 READ MORE: Ex-All Blacks forward makes Hurricanes return as Super Rugby champions confirm new coaching hires It wasn't long ago that Beauden Barrett's Rugby World Cup hopes were in doubt. Mike Blair has revealed how important the experienced playmaking duo Beauden Barrett and Damian McKenzie are to the All Blacks' cause on attack. Beauden Barrett has struggled for most of 2026 but a positional switch has certainly helped the All Blacks legend. Sir Graham Henry admits that Beauden Barrett has dispelled the doubts he had over the veteran All Blacks' future. © Planet Sport Limited 2026 • All Rights Reserved

title: Arsenal 1-0 Hull City: How the players rated - BBC
content: Odegaard hits winner as Arsenal beat Hull to extend lead at top Arsenal needed a late goal from Martin Odegaard to beat a stubborn Hull side at Emirates Stadium. The Gunners, who thought they should have been awarded a penalty in the first half, looked like they would be frustrated by the Tigers before Odegaard followed up Noni Madueke's shot to tap in the winner. Here's how I rated the players and you can see how you scored them below. David Raya: A good save when Elliot Stroud drilled a low cross into the area. 6 Jurrien Timber: Not his best game in an Arsenal shirt. 5 Ezri Konsa: Another good performance, which is what is expected from him since signing for the Gunners. 7 Gabriel Magalhaes: Caught on the ball once in the middle of the pitch but the usual solid performance apart from that. 7 Riccardo Calafiori: A good defensive performance but not his usual impact when going forward. 6 Declan Rice: Went closest for Arsenal in the first half with an effort from the edge of the box but subbed as Arsenal chased a goal. 6 Bruno Guimaraes: The midfielder still seems to be getting up to the pace of the season. 6 Martin Odegaard: Scored the crucial goal for Arsenal. Injected pace into the Arsenal play whenever he got on the ball and deserved to score the winner. 8 Christos Tzolis: Lots of energy but not much quality from the winger. 5 Noni Madueke: A dangerous ball in followed by a driving run early in the game. Alongside Odegaard the winger was Arsenal's main threat and his shot resulted in the winner. 7 Kai Havertz: Disappointing first half and turned back instead of shooting when played through. Went down after a shirt pull for a penalty but was given offside after a VAR check. A poor performance. 4 Gyokeres (on 63, Havertz): Did not make much of an impact. 5 Merino (on 63, Rice): A calming influence when he came on. 6 Eze (on 69, Tzolis): Added some flair to the Arsenal attack. 6 Hincapie (on 69, Calafiori): A more traditional left back and overlapped as Arsenal pushed for the win. 6 Subs not used: Arrizabalaga, White, Mosquera, Lewis-Skelly. Konstantinos Tzolakis: Pushed Madueke's shot back into a dangerous area which resulted in the goal. 7 Lewie Coyle: A solid performance but replaced on the hour mark as Arsenal piled on the pressure. 6 Semi Ajayi: The centre-back seemed to be in the way of a lot of what came into the Hull penalty area. Came off with an injury. 7 John Egan: An early chance from a corner and had his head in his hands afterwards, which suggests he feels he could have done better. Defended well. 7 Nobel Mendy: Perhaps lucky to get away with a shirt pull on Havertz but defended well apart from that. 6 Elliot Stroud: Forced Raya into a smart stop with a dangerous delivery into the box. Struggled with the threat of Madueke. 5 Tim Iroegbunam: Worked hard to break up the Arsenal play and subbed late on. 6 Lucas Gourna-Douath: A real calming presence in the middle of the pitch for Hull. Shielded the back four but tired as Arsenal pushed for the win. 6 Mohamed-Ali Cho: Lots of runs behind the Arsenal backline, taken off in the second half. 6 Oli McBurnie: Battled all afternoon against the physically dominant Konsa and Gabriel. 6 Gelhardt (on 60, Cho): Introduced a threat down the right wing. 6 Norton-Cuffy: (on 61, Coyle): Booked after making his first tackle. Under a lot of pressure as faced with Eze. 6 Herrington: (on 69, Ajayi): Replaced Ajayi and Hull conceded soon after. 6 After the opportunity to rate players has closed, the score displayed represents the average from all the submissions by BBC Sport users.
