title: Scotland v New Zealand: Five takeaways as All Blacks pass litmus test with 'flying colours' despite benefitting from 'clear and obvious' obsession - Planet Rugby
content: All Blacks back-rower Wallace Sititi and an inset of Scotland hooker Ewan Ashman. Following the All Blacks’ 43-21 victory over Scotland, here are our five takeaways from the Nations Championship clash at Murrayfield. Dave Rennie’s men continued their winning streak in the inaugural Nations Championship and maintained their unbeaten run at the home of Scottish Rugby courtesy of a ruthless attacking display and a second-half shutout. The set-pieces took centre stage today, with the tries flowing in the first half from the lineouts, the first coming through Wallace Sititi with the back-rower charging away after a dummy carry from Peter Lakai. It was a statement of intent from the visitors after just three minutes but the Scots’ reply was swift as Kyle Rowe expertly dissected the All Blacks‘ backfield with a pinpoint 50:22. From the ensuing lineout, Ewan Ashman got his first five points of the afternoon and there was more of that in store for the hooker. Ethan de Groot was next to cross the whitewash with the prop forward benefitting from a smart kick and the immense work-rate of Beauden Barrett who won a penalty inside the Scottish 22. Scrum-half Cam Roigard quickly tapped the ball and moments later it was the Highlanders loosehead who powered over. Lakai went from providing the deception for Sititi’s score to grabbing five points of his own as New Zealand went into a 17-7 lead but the flanker was sent to the sin bin soon after, which gave Scotland an opportunity to counterpunch, which they duly did. Sione Tuipulotu pulled the strings along with Finn Russell, with Ashman making the final carry to score his second try. Despite being down a man, the All Blacks had a reply and through the most experienced man on the pitch as Beauden Barrett latched onto a Damian McKenzie flat pass to score his 49th Test try to extend the visitors’ lead to 24-14. Sititi would replicate Lakai in scoring a try and visiting the sin bin when he was yellow-carded in the 32nd minute and whilst he was off the pitch, Ashman created history by becoming the first Scotsman to score a hat-trick against the mighty All Blacks. That meant that Gregor Townsend’s men trailed by only three points after a helter-skelter first half but the second 40 minutes belonged to the men in black. Josh Moorby got the scoreboard ticking again just eight minutes after the break as he benefited from a dominant scrum, and Barrett followed two minutes later to complete his brace and bring up 50 Test tries – becoming only the second player to do so for the All Blacks after Will Jordan. The Scots attacked ferociously but not accurately as New Zealand’s defence held firm and the game was put to bed and well beyond reach in the 67th minute as replacement hooker Asafo Aumua raced away for a try. There is an obsession from Australia and New Zealand that the TMO should only intervene when the action is clear and obvious, which World Rugby has opted in its protocol for the fourth officials. In fact, Rennie even weighed in on the potential of the TMO’s intervention earlier this week after naming his team. He predicted that the stoppages for reviews would differ from match to match depending on the officiating team. Today, Andrew Brace was willing to let TMO Olly Hodges make decisions in the background, trusting that he would get them right without his intervention. The All Blacks benefitted from that and the need to only intervene when it is clear and obvious when it came to Sititi’s try off the back of a suspect set-move from a driving maul. New Zealand set the maul outside the Scottish 22 and at the back, Lakai broke away without the ball and towards the opposition’s midfield with Sititi following shortly after as he carried closer to the maul with ball in hand and scored. It was a brilliant bit of deception, a move the All Blacks have used before and Leinster deployed against Connacht recently but is it legal? Law 16.11 concerning this reads: “During a maul players must not: (c) Take any action to make opponents believe that the maul has ended when it has not.” Making this call live is nigh on impossible for Brace, but it would be something that could be reviewed; but Hodges clearly felt that there was not clear and obvious evidence to bring it to the referee’s attention. Brace could have called for a review himself, but again, World Rugby are attempting to keep the game flowing and New Zealand are one of the nations who are pressing that they do so. Would Brace have viewed the decision differently had an official review occurred? We will never know. Reviewing the footage, Lakai and Sititi certainly don’t break off simultaneously, but it was nip and tuck. Italy v South Africa: Winners and losers as ‘rising star’ shines for Springboks while Azzurri playmaker ‘fails miserably’ in defeat Before today, only four players had ever scored a hat-trick against the All Blacks: Australia’s Greg Cornelsen, South Africa’s Ray Mordt and Marius Joubert, and Wales’ Tom Rogers, with Cornelsen being the only to score four in one match. However, that number grew to five at Murrayfield as Scotland hooker Ashman went over three times in the first half. The front-rower will surely be asked to buy around from his fellow forwards and should probably oblige, as two of his three came from the work of his fellow pack men. Ashman still deserves credit for his ability to finish off the opportunities that came his way. The first was classic hooker play at the back of a driving maul, the second was a sharp line that he ran to deliver the killer blow on an All Blacks’ defence that was reeling, and the third was a well-timed breakaway from the back of the maul to score. The Scotsman is also the second forward to score three against the men in black and the first in 48 years – Cornelsen becoming the first-ever player to do so. The hooker has certainly benefitted from the stricter officiating around the mauls, but that should not take away from his special achievement today. Springboks player ratings: ‘Mammoth’ Malcolm Marx leads Italian mauling as ‘swaggering’ Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu shines This fixture wasn’t nearly as close as it was 12 months ago, with the All Blacks ultimately pulling away from Townsend’s men and blowing them away in the second half. What played in New Zealand’s favour this time around was just how much rugby this team has played together recently after Rugby’s Greatest Rivalry series and the Bledisloe Cup. Conversely, this Scottish side hasn’t played together since the July Nations Championship matches. The cohesion was perhaps most evident in the opportunities that the visitors took and the ones that the hosts didn’t. Rennie’s side averaged a touch over three points per entry into the Scottish 22, Townsend’s men averaged less than two and a half. The Scots didn’t lack opportunities, making nine entries but routinely spilled the ball or wasted chances to score points. That ruthlessness comes with cohesion but the Tana Umaga-coached defence deserves its credit too, as the All Blacks were excellent in patches and particularly in their red zone. It’s worth noting that all but one of Scotland’s tries came through the set-piece, with the outlier being a prolonged period in possession and a systematic breakdown of the defence over multiple facets of the play, and those do happen. Italy v Springboks: Five takeaways as ‘ice-cold’ South Africa floor Azzurri but why Rassie Erasmus won’t be happy ahead of French ‘grudge match’ The improvements in the All Blacks scrum were evident against the Springboks in the latter stages of Rugby’s Greatest Rivalry series and then again in the Bledisloe Cup versus the Wallabies. However, Scotland posed a different challenge, a team that revels in the set-piece battle, but Rennie’s big men not only rose to the challenge but thrived. It took some time, but in the second half, the All Blacks really turned the screws and put the hosts under pressure, so much so that they opted for a scrum from a penalty, and Moorby reaped the rewards from the strong platform set by the pack. New Zealand have always been a competent scrummaging nation at worst, and at times dominant, but earlier this year it was an Achilles ‘ heel for the team. The improvements have been slow, but today felt like a statement performance from the men up front that the All Blacks scrum is turning the corner and getting back to the highs that it was once at. There was even a hunger to pack down in the scrum, courtesy of tighthead Fletcher Newell, who asked Andrew Brace whether they could re-pack the set-piece inside New Zealand’s 22 from a free-kick instead of kicking – sorry Fletcher, you can thank World Rugby for the answer being no. We marked this match as a litmus test for the New Zealand scrum and they very clearly passed it with flying colours. What was plainly evident is that the All Blacks are a different beast when the scrum is operating well and so is the lineout, with their tries all coming from the set-pieces. title: Recap: All Blacks beat Scotland, remain unbeaten in Nations Championship - NZ Herald
content:

How the action unfolded as the All Blacks beat Scotland 43-21 at Murrayfield It’s time New Zealand paid Scottish rugby due respect. Maybe it’s historical
arrogance forged on the All Blacks’ 121-year unbeaten record against the Scots. Maybe the misleading, irrelevant World Rugby rankings. Whatever the cause, Kiwis are often too quick to assume, too ready to dismiss, Scotland’s genuine threat. Nothing lasts for ever. Just ask Ireland and Argentina, two teams to smash their glass ceiling against the All Blacks in recent years. This generation of Scottish rugby is a world away from the easybeat teams the All Blacks humbled 62-31 in 1996, 69-20 in 2000, both at Carisbrook in Dunedin, or 40-0 in the 2007 World Cup pool stages and 51-22 in 2012 at Murrayfield. In the last 12 years, three of the past four tests between the All Blacks and Scotland at Murrayfield were decided by eight points, the other by five, to paint the true tale of the locals’ improvement. In recent times, particularly last year when they blew large leads against the All Blacks and Argentina at home, Gregor Townsend should have delivered more from Scotland. At this point, Scotland are yet to shake their nearly men tag while continuing to promise more. This year Scotland mustered three Six Nations wins including putting 50 points on the full-strength French at Murrayfield and defeating England to preserve an unbeaten home record this season. In July they pushed the Springboks in South Africa and knocked off the Pumas in Argentina to sit second, behind France, in the northern hemisphere Nations Championship table. Questions persist about Scotland’s ability to deliver repeat performances, to summon the decisive killer instinct, and whether they truly believe they can topple the All Blacks. Yet their backline threats alone – Finn Russell, arguably the world’s premier playmaker, classy British and Irish Lions midfielders Sione Tuipulotu and Huw Jones, dubbed ‘Huwipulotu’, and wing Kyle Steyn – can amass points quickly. With such generational talents in fine fettle, those flocking to the iconic Murrayfield again dare to dream. Doubts remain about whether this is their day, their moment, to savour history but Scotland may well prove a tougher test than England as cultural turmoil – akin to the internal ructions that ended Scott Robertson’s All Blacks reign – engulfs Steve Borthwick’s shaky tenure. Regardless of the result this Sunday morning (NZT), the time has come for New Zealanders to etch overdue respect on the Scottish rugby crest. External confidence for a famous upset in Edinburgh appears low as there is widespread recognition that the All Blacks are in a much better place than this time last year when the Robertson regime disintegrated at the seams. While this season is stress testing depth, with nine players ruled out for the year, the All Blacks’ revived attacking strike and demands for ferocious physicality at the breakdown signpost their marked improvements. Perhaps more importantly, though, they are fully aligned and united which should mitigate against another Murrayfield meltdown such as blowing a 17-point halftime lead and conceding three second-half yellow cards here last November. “They’re quite different from last year,” Scotland coach Gregor Townsend noted. “They’re playing more ambitious rugby and have a real sense of unity.” Of their starting team to confront the All Blacks, five of Scotland’s side do not play for Glasgow Warriors. Three of those five – Australian No 8 Jack Dempsey, Russell and Jones – previously played for Glasgow. Three more Glasgow figures populate Scotland’s bench. On the one hand such an extended cohort from one team allows Townsend to draw on established combinations and cohesion. On the other, it gifts former Glasgow coaches Dave Rennie and Mike Blair a dossier of inside knowledge and, surely, a competitive advantage. Blair is as Scottish as they come. He grew up in Edinburgh before progressing to become Scotland’s most capped international halfback. More pertinent for this week, though, Rennie and Blair spent three years together coaching Glasgow. They know the Scottish rugby landscape, the mentality, passion, style, player tendencies and conditions, intimately. That matters. This week Rennie recalled handing Kyle Steyn his first start in the midfield at Glasgow – and that’s merely one example. “It’s been nice to sit back and look from afar at a number of those guys who we had at Glasgow kick on ... maybe not so good in the weekend, hopefully.” Rennie’s familiarity with Scotland and the people extended to attending an event with Glasgow sponsors and staff this week. “I had three great years here and loved it. We had a bit of a Q&A with Ryan Wilson and Mike Blair. We did a thing for a lot of the Glasgow sponsors and so on. It was really good to see a lot of the staff and a number of the ex-players turned up. They’re great people so it’s nice to be back.” The sudden death of Logan Cadwallader, the All Blacks’ head of security and former Special Air Service soldier, last Sunday in Edinburgh cast a sombre cloud over the team this week. Cadwallader had been with the All Blacks for a decade. During that time he formed close bonds with past and present players and management that stretched far beyond touring duties to leave everyone involved hit hard by his passing. Earlier this week the All Blacks acknowledged his passing and allowed everyone time to grieve before attempting to channel that emotion. The team will don black armbands to acknowledge Cadwallader against Scotland, and they are determined to honour his service with a performance he would be proud of. “We’ve certainly talked about that. He wouldn’t be happy with us moping around all week and struggling to put in a performance,” Rennie said. “It’s been a tough few days. He’s such a good man, he meant a helluva lot to the team so there’s been a big emotional toll. We’ve had his brother Dwayne here and his best mate Nathan so it’s been a chance to get together and share stories. That’s helped, but it’s really rocked the squad. Our thoughts are with Nannette and the kids.” Liam Napier is a Senior Sports Journalist and Rugby Correspondent for the New Zealand Herald. He is a co-host of the Rugby Direct podcast. title: Italy v South Africa: Winners and losers as 'rising star' shines for Springboks while Azzurri playmaker 'fails miserably' in defeat - Planet Rugby
content: Italy fly-half Paolo Garbisi and Springboks scrum-half  Morne van den Berg had contrasting fortunes in Turin. Following the Springboks’ 66-7 triumph over Italy in their Nations Championship Test, here are our winners and losers from Saturday’s encounter at the Allianz Stadium. From the outset, the Springboks fly-half had a spring in his step and after kicking an early penalty he took the fight to the home side as he showed off his vast array of skills which created several try-scoring opportunities for the world champions. Feinberg-Mngomezulu hit the ground running in Turin as he delivered a 100 per cent goal-kicking performance and apart from that penalty, he also slotted nine conversions while showing his class on attack as he crossed for his team’s first try in the eighth minute. Aside from that, the young playmaker also showed his class when he delivered a well-weighted 50/22 kick from close to his 22-metre line and the ball went into touch close to Italy‘s try-line. Not far behind Feinberg-Mngomezulu was his half-back partner Van den Berg, who continued with his excellent form from earlier in the year for the world champions and produced another top class all-round performance. The nippy scrum-half was in the thick of the action as he kicked accurately out of hand, provided a slick service to his outside backs and controlled the tempo of the match as he varied his play intelligently. Van den Berg‘s attacking brilliance saw him crossing for a well-taken try during the opening half and he continued to keep his side on the front foot with his superb distribution skills as the match progressed. The Boks’ rising star’s efforts were rewarded with the official player-of-the-match award after the game. The young utility back came into the Springboks’ run-on side as a replacement for the great Cheslin Kolbe during the latter part of Rugby’s Greatest Rivalry series against the All Blacks and impressed with a solid performance in the final Test in Baltimore. Hooker continued where he left off in that match against the Azzurri as he shone on either side of the ball and led the way in the aerial battle for the world champions where he won several duels. He eventually finished with a match-high 92 metres gained and just like the corresponding fixture at the same venue last year, he crossed for a deserved try after the full-time hooter. While the Springboks’ entire forward pack delivered another excellent performance which set a superb platform for their backs, Marx deserves special praise as he showed why he is the current World Rugby Player of the Year. The Bulls-bound hooker was only on the field for 46 minutes but was hugely influential during that period as he shone in the execution of his core duties with his lineout throw-ins particularly impressive and he delivered a 100 per cent return in that department. Marx also made a big impact with ball in hand and crossed for two tries to extend his record to 31 five-pointers which is the most by any South African forward at international level. Although the Azzurri are regarded as the Springboks’ weakest opponents on their European tour – with France and Ireland still lying in wait – Erasmus opted to field a strong matchday squad with the bulk of his regular first-choice players named in the starting line-up and that decision certainly paid off. From the outset, the world champions showed that they meant business as they dominated most facets of play and they delivered a near-perfect performance in the first half which saw them holding a 45-0 lead at the interval. After half-time, Italy were more competitive, but the damage was done and Erasmus rang the changes with several of his star players replaced. Italy v Springboks: Five takeaways as ‘ice-cold’ South Africa floor Azzurri but why Rassie Erasmus won’t be happy ahead of French ‘grudge match’ As the scoreline suggests, there were few positives for the home side from this clash but rookie blindside flanker Ortombina can be proud of his efforts although that was made mostly on defence. With the world champions running rampant with ball in hand, Ortombina did not shirk when executing his defensive duties and he really put his body on the line in that department. And after 80 minutes, it was not surprising that the 24-year-old emerged with a match-high 20 tackles made which will certainly enhance his chances of retaining his spot in Italy’s run-on side during the rest of the Nations Championship. There was a big responsibility on the Azzurri’s chief playmaker’s shoulders as he was expected to give his team direction but, unfortunately, he failed miserably with that task. Although he received scrappy ball from his forwards, Garbisi failed to influence proceedings and early in the second half he had an embarrassing moment when he failed to put the ball out from a routine kick for touch after Italy were awarded a penalty on the Boks’ 22-metre line. It was not a surprise when he was eventually replaced after 61 minutes with Tommaso Allan coming on to take his place. The Azzurri were without several of their first-choice players which meant there was more pressure on the more experienced players in their run-on side for this clash with Stade Francais hooker Nicotera being one of those as the team’s captain. However, this will not be a match which he will remember fondly as he had little influence on proceedings. The 30-year-old failed to find his jumpers in the lineouts on a couple of occasions and made little impact on attack and defence. Despite being his side’s skipper, Nicotera was only on the field for 48 minutes of this match before being replaced by Tommaso Di Bartolomeo. Another one of the home side’s experienced players of whom much was expected but he failed to deliver the goods. The hard running number eight is usually one of the players who gives the Azzurri good momentum with ball in hand but that wasn’t the case in this match as he was kept in check by the visitors’ defence. Although he put in a solid defensive display, as he made 10 hits, he only gained eight attacking metres and was eventually replaced by Ross Vintcent after 54 minutes. Want more from Planet Rugby? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for world-class coverage you can trust. The La Rochelle second-row was a surprise inclusion in the Springboks’ starting line-up as he was the only player in the run-on side who was not involved in their recent 3-1 series triumph against the All Blacks. Moerat’s selection for the Boks usually receives plenty of criticism on social media which led to Erasmus launching a passionate defence of the 28-year-old when he announced his team earlier in the week. That meant Moerat’s call-up for this encounter presented him with the perfect opportunity to justify his selection and, in doing so, silence his critics as well but that did not happen as he was a late withdrawal in the build-up to this game due to a back injury. That meant Lood de Jager was promoted to the run-on side while Franco Mostert was added to the replacements bench. title: Chelsea Women v Everton Women | Match | Official Site - Chelsea Football Club
content: With a defensive record only bettered by Chelsea in the WSL this season, the Blues knew we would be in for a tough afternoon against Everton even before the match had kicked off, and so it proved as we had to settle for a point at Stamford Bridge. After a cagey first half hour, Sandy Baltimore broke the deadlock when a small connection on the ball saw her steer home from a Lucy Bronze header back across goal. It felt like Chelsea were on our way, but when Bronze took an unfortunate touch from a looping ball in, the Toffees were back on level terms just four minutes later, and the teams went in at 1-1 at the break. Despite Everton not managing a shot on target during the match, the visitors made things really difficult for the Blues, reducing us to half-chances throughout. Their efforts were rewarded as they kept us from adding to the scoreline and took a point away from the Bridge. Sonia Bompastor made four alterations to her starting XI, swapping Veerle Buurman, Nathalie Bjorn and Sjoeke Nusken for Bronze, Kadeisha Buchanan and Erin Cuthbert. Lauren James had unfortunately been ruled out with a hamstring injury earlier in the week, and Wieke Kaptein came into the line-up in her place. The head coach had mentioned in her pre-match press conference that she expected the visitors to defend well, and that's exactly what happened in the opening stages of the game as the Toffees played in a compact formation as they attempted to negate our strengths. Our first real attempt came from one of Ellie Carpenter's trademark runs down the flank, and as she let fly with a shot, only a tiny deflection from the defender saw it bounce just wide of the right-hand post. Melvine Malard was next to go close with a header that was just off target, but the offside flag went up soon afterwards to confirm that it wouldn't have counted. It wasn't going to be easy to break Everton down, but the Blues were getting closer. After a superb one-two with Carpenter, Kaptein blasted her shot towards goal but had her attempt cleared off the line. Our opener came soon afterwards. After we took a short corner, Katie McCabe swung a cross into the back post to find the head of Bronze. The centre-back cushioned her header across the face of goal, allowing Baltimore to nod home with the slightest of touches. Yet the Toffees hit back when a looping cross from Yuka Momiki took an unfortunate touch off Bronze and deflected into the back of the net. Our number 22 almost cancelled out the own goal with a bullet header seven minutes before the break, but an impressive stop saw Everton goalkeeper Courtney Brosnan tip the attempt over the bar. After another tight opening to the second half, Bompastor made a double substitution after 55 minutes, introducing Nusken and Thompson for Baltimore and Kaptein. The clock ticked towards 70 and, other than a series of corners, the Blues were yet to put any real pressure on a resolute Everton defence. When the Blues were awarded a free-kick for a late challenge on Carpenter, McCabe took it short to Thompson just outside her, and the American laid the ball off to Walsh. The midfielder bent in a curling shot, but Brosnan was able to collect. That was the only real danger we caused in the second half as the statistics showed we fired 21 shots on goal but ended the match with only three big chances created. It was a frustrating day, but we will look to regain top spot when we face leaders Manchester City next weekend in the WSL. We drop to second in the table, two points behind leaders Manchester City, following their 5-0 win over West Ham United earlier today. We travel to Sweden to face Hacken in the Women's Champions League on Tuesday, with kick-off set for 5.45pm UK time. We will then back at Stamford Bridge for our top-of-the-table clash with Man City next Saturday. Tickets are still available and you can secure your place here. title: Leeds United v Tottenham Hotspur : How the players rated - BBC
content: Leeds United's Nico Elvedi challenges Spurs striker Omar Marmoush in the Premier League game at Elland Road Leeds United ended Spurs' mini-revival with a late goal from Noah Okafor giving them victory at Elland Road. Here's how I rated the players - and you can see how you scored them below. James Trafford: Always alert coming off his line when danger threatened. Safe handling. Vital late save from Van Hecke in the closing moments. 6 James Justin: Good deliveries and solid in defence. 6 Nico Elvedi: Won his physical battle with Marmoush. Headed a good chance wide. 6 Tarik Muharemovic: Very solid display. A bargain. 6 Jayden Bogle: Good going forward but can consider himself very fortunate not to get a red card for a late challenge on Mathys Tel. 5 Ethan Ampadu: Leeds United's captain kept things ticking over in midfield and always a strong presence. 7 Sean Longstaff: Booking for a late challenge on Fernandes. Saw a close-range effort saved. 6 Ao Tanaka: Worked hard but missed a great second-half opportunity. 6 Gabriel Gudmundsson: Excellent first half with some lively runs. Shame he had to come off at half-time. 7 Dominic Calvert-Lewin: Hard-working and unselfish when he set up Tanaka for a chance he should have taken. 6 Lukas Nmecha: Struggling. Headed straight at Kinsky when he should have scored. 5 Melvin Bard (on 45, Gudmundsson): Some fine forward passes in a decent display. 6 Noah Okafor (on 77, Lukas Nmecha). Inspirational substitution by Daniel Farke. Clean finish two minutes after coming on. 7 Harry Wilson (on 77, Ao Tanaka). Tried to create. 5 Subs not used: Michael Zetterer, Jaka Bijol, Daniel James, Brenden Aaronson. De Zerbi focuses on Spurs' failings - but should Bogle have seen red? Antonin Kinsky: Very safe handling and excellent save from Longstaff. No chance with the goal. Anxious moment when he took too long over a goal-kick and a corner was awarded. 7 Pedro Porro: Always willing to join the attack. Loves a tackle but probably taken off to avoid a red card. 6 Micky van de Ven: Dependable presence at the heart of the Spurs defence. One vital second-half clearance. Booked for hauling back Bogle. 6 Jan Paul van Hecke: One of his best games for Spurs. Powerful in the air and composed with the ball at his feet. Almost saved a point at the end. 7 Andrew Robertson: Solid defensively and always energetic in lending weight to attack. 6 Archie Gray: Some nice touches against his old club but generally quiet. 6 Mateus Fernandes: Very quiet. No influence at all. 5 Mohammed Kudus: Lots of endeavour but little end product. 5 Omar Marmoush: Poor. Lacked physical presence against Leeds' defenders. 5 Mathys Tel: One or two lively moments but unable to continue after Jayden Bogle's poor first-half challenge. 5 Dominic Solanke (on 43, Tel): Crucial block from Calvert-Lewin. No attacking effect. 5 Conor Gallagher (on 65, Porro): Shot inches wide. 5 Rodrigo Bentacur (on 65, Mateus Fernandes): Little impact. Missed chance in the final seconds. 5 Dejan Kulusevski (on 65, Omar Marmoush): Kept at bay by Leeds. 5 Subs not used: Luca Gunter, Marcos Senesi, James Maddison, Ben Davies. title: Italy v Springboks: Five takeaways as 'ice-cold' South Africa floor Azzurri but why Rassie Erasmus won't be happy ahead of French 'grudge match' - Planet Rugby
content: Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu impressed for the Springboks. South Africa’s flawless opening 40 minutes delivered 45 points on the way to a 66-7 win in Turin, as Juventus’s home witnessed near-perfect rugby that left the Azzurri without a single dominant carry until the second half. This was always going to be a pretty steep mountain to climb at the foot of the Alps, as a Springbok 23 carrying around 1,000 caps started the second half of their Nations Championship campaign in Turin, but it’s fair to say nobody, not even the most diehard Bok fan, expected the climb to be this steep for the hosts. Just after the half-hour South Africa had six tries, all converted, and a 45-0 lead, and in that first half Italy made no dominant carries and only one dominant tackle, and they didn’t touch the ball in open play in the Springbok 22 until Leonardo Marin got his hands on it in first-half added time, from a kick, whereupon Italy promptly knocked it on. You rarely see a half of Test rugby like that. It was simple, calculated, flawless, elite, ice-cold Test rugby from a side that won every collision, found every gap and took every opportunity that presented itself, and frankly the rest of the tournament, and Italy in particular, may wish to petition World Rugby for a new blue card, allowing sympathy reinforcements for whoever happens to be facing the Springboks when they’re in this mood. The second half was a different story, in fairness to Italy, 21-7 to the Boks but with a flurry of errors after the break, as six replacements came on in one go, Rassie Erasmus well aware that Paris is only six days away, and the Italian bench gave the Azzurri something to hold on to. Will South Africa be happy? In the final analysis, no. Erasmus wants that level of first-half perfection for 80 minutes, not 40, and today South Africa were brilliant for one half and a shadow of themselves in the second. The foundation was the collision. Every single Springbok carry gained two or three metres after contact, whilst every Italian carry went backwards, and by half-time the numbers were brutal: South Africa had carried 37 times for 252 metres to Italy’s 13 carries for 60. Stats like that are rare at this level, and with the Springboks owning 65 per cent of the ball and 60 per cent of the territory, Italy barely had a touch, and when they did, they went backwards a great deal faster than they ever managed to go forwards. Defensively South Africa were peerless, holding their width, which meant Italy had no space outside and had to carry into contact. Once they did, the Springbok tacklers isolated the carrier before his support could get there, and whilst it didn’t produce a flood of breakdown steals, it produced spills, knock-ons and errors galore; in that first quarter Italy knocked on [seven] times and conceded six penalties, plus a yellow card for Muhamed Hasa for a deliberate knock-on. Penalties are bodies, and Italy were giving them away because they were losing every single moment of contact. Springboks player ratings: ‘Mammoth’ Malcolm Marx leads Italian mauling as ‘swaggering’ Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu shines On the other side of the ball it was all about ruck speed. South Africa won all 36 of their rucks in the first half, and the ball came back so quickly that Italy could never get numbers back into the line once they’d committed bodies to the floor, which shows palpably how a side can be patient and ruthless at the same time. The Boks simply went through the phases until the gap appeared, patient, poised and ice-cold. Italy did well to stop the first lineout maul on 16 minutes, but Morne van den Berg flew over from the side of the next ruck, and Malcolm Marx went on to score twice from lineout drives, the second when the Azzurri were down to 14 men. To be fair to Italy, they aren’t a bad side, and there were a couple of things to hold on to. Their scrum held at times, especially when Simone Ferrari was on, Paolo Odogwu defended well and they stopped that first maul, but their attack had no shape, the errors kept coming and their exit strategy was at times diabolical, handing the ball straight back to South Africa, largely because the Springbok line speed rushed Paolo Garbisi into error after error. Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu‘s try inside the first ten minutes set the tone, a third-phase break that left Giacomo Nicotera and Alessandro Fusco for dead as he spotted a gap between the two defenders and lit the afterburners for a 40-metre run to the line, made entirely by his own vision and fleetness of foot. Watching it was like playing tennis against Novak Djokovic and, having won a set off him, hearing him announce he’s been playing left-handed all along. That’s how big the mismatch was. Then, from the restart after Marx’s first try, Feinberg-Mngomezulu kicked a 50:22 straight from his own exit, and Siya Kolisi went over from the lineout to wrap up the bonus point inside the first 25 minutes. He wasn’t flawless, knocking on twice either side of half-time, once on his own 22, but those were the first blemishes of a brilliant afternoon. What stood out most was the decision-making, an all-court game in which the Boks picked the right option almost every time, built on patience, practice, belief and understanding. The practice was obvious on Italy’s contestable kicks, where South Africa tactically put two men on the kicking side of the Italian receiver, so that any ball tapped back fell straight into their arms, and by the hour mark they’d managed it six times; it was like taking sweets off a toddler. That doesn’t happen by accident, and Erasmus can now consider himself officially redundant, because his players are coaching themselves on the field, which is exactly what elite coaches want to see. Van den Berg took the official player of the match award, and his kicking game is certainly the best of the Springbok options right now, especially when he’s lucky enough to have Ethan Hooker in his chasing pack. Feinberg-Mngomezulu, Hooker or Van den Berg, any of the three could have been player of the match. Hooker was outstanding; he popped up at 13, won the ball in the air and finished the ninth try late on after the Springbok scrum drove Italy back in a heap. Opposing centres will be glad he’s on the wing, because he’s massive, quick and has fabulous hands, with a cut-out pass that would make Ignacio Brex smile, and the numbers back it up: Hooker made 86 metres and six clean breaks, comfortably the most on the pitch. South Africa’s second innings was a stumbling affair by comparison, and the cricketers amongst the Springbok fans might suggest the Juventus pitch was starting to turn as the day wore on. The Boks made more errors in the first five minutes after the break, with knock-ons from Feinberg-Mngomezulu, Kurt-Lee Arendse and Damian Willemse, than in the whole first half, and as the replacements came on en masse the edge came off the South African game. Italy, to their credit, improved, and it was a bit of both, an Azzurri side finding some passion, some pride and something to play for, whilst South Africa eased off a little amid the changes from the bench. Early in the second half Ferrari’s scrum drove the Boks back into their own 22 and won a penalty, and if Ox Nche has one tighthead who matches him almost blow for blow and is prepared to go toe to toe with him, it’s Ferrari. Italy then missed touch from 15 metres, undoing all the great work of their pack, an absolute coach-killer. Their first dominant carry didn’t come until Ross Vintcent managed one well into the second half, but debutant Samuele Locatelli and Marin followed, and soon after a dominant carry in midfield off a lineout drew the Springbok defence narrow and a training-ground switch put Federico Ruzza over in the corner. It’s key to understand that Italy needed to win a collision first, something they’d continually failed to do. The bench made a big difference. Stephen Varney, Vintcent and Manuel Zuliani, who won a penalty on the floor, lifted the tempo, and Enoch Opoku-Gyamfi made Italy’s second dominant tackle, on Franco Mostert, around the 50-minute mark. Italy finished with six turnovers won to South Africa’s two, and Fusco, with five defenders beaten and a clean break, was their most dangerous runner, despite a poor kicking game by his standards. After a first half like that, Gonzalo Quesada’s best course is to forget the first 40 completely and focus on what he can take from the second. The lesson he can’t ignore, however, is about selection, because the replacements well and truly outplayed the men they replaced, with Vintcent, Zuliani and Varney all giving him compelling reasons to start them in Genoa, whilst of the starters only Ange Capuozzo and Ferrari can hold their heads up high, having done anything near a Test-match job. The half-backs need a rethink too, because a side that has the ball as rarely as Italy did simply can’t afford to keep kicking it away, and they have to get their exits and touch-finders right, which neither starter managed today. Argentina will offer a very different test, and judging by Los Pumas’ lineout and set-piece misery in Dublin last night, Italy’s maul and Ferrari’s scrummaging could be genuine weapons to push the South Americans all the way. For South Africa, Erasmus will be happiest that his squad came through the 80 minutes fit, but he’ll look for a big improvement in the second half, an area where South Africa have traditionally been very strong, not least this summer. They face France in Paris on Friday, one of the biggest grudge matches in Test rugby, before finishing the series against Ireland in Dublin on 21 November. title: England v Wallabies prediction: Steve Borthwick's side to have 'just enough' to win as hosts pass 'acid test' for November block - Planet Rugby
content: Ben Earl (left) and Harry Wilson (right) will meet in England v Australia this weekend England and Australia are set to resume their storied rivalry this weekend, as both sides seek to land a sucker punch in the Nations Championship opener on Sunday. This feels a pivotal Test for both sides, as they look to show their recent improvements are no flash in the pan. England come into the upcoming block finally back to winning ways, after two victories against Fiji and Argentina, but before that had endured their worst-ever Six Nations campaign and lost to the Springboks in their July Nations Championship opener. The Wallabies, meanwhile, seem to have found a new lease of life under new boss Les Kiss, and they sit on a record of five wins from seven in his tenure. However, those two defeats have come in their most recent outings, falling to an aggregate loss of 93-40 against the All Blacks in the Bledisloe Cup Tests. But this is a chance for both sides to really lay down a marker moving into the rest of the Nations Championship, and a win for either side could really act as a catapult towards the top of their respective pools. England are currently fourth in the Northern Hemisphere table after three Tests, but a win on Sunday plus results elsewhere falling their way could move them up to the top of the tree. Australia are third in the Southern Hemisphere pool at the time of writing, but while they are unable to climb up any places, could close the gap on both the All Blacks and Springboks with a victory. The sides are not unfamiliar to each other, either, with them meeting for the third successive year at Allianz Stadium, Twickenham, with Australia winning in 2024 and England getting revenge in 2025. There are probably a lot of interesting mini-battles within this game. England’s power game got them over the line against the Wallabies last year, while Australia’s desire to play out wide helped them to victory in 2024. England team: Winners and losers as Steve Borthwick ‘puts faith’ in forward pair while head coach ‘misses opportunity’ with returning duo’s omission This time around, though, it feels like the breakdown is going to be the main differential. Australia’s defensive system is almost built around being able to compete at the ruck, often leaving at least one for their back-rowers floating around the tackle to clamp down on the ball and win a turnover. It’s also the sheer speed of how messers Fraser McReight and Harry Wilson can get there that should worry England the most. But Steve Borthwick isn’t short of top breakdown operators either. His selection of Ben Curry at open side is a clear indication he will target this area, while Ben Earl, Maro Itoje and even replacement Henry Pollock are top operators in it as well. The breakdown is going to be a fascinating sub-plot to this contest. ﻿ Speaking ahead of the game, England boss Borthwick outlined his side are fully aware of the challenge ahead of them this weekend: “Australia are a talented side who have played a significant amount of Test rugby in recent months. We know the challenge that awaits us and we’re looking forward to it. “We’re excited to be playing in front of our home supporters and to start an important block of games. This will also be our last opportunity to face southern hemisphere opposition at home before the World Cup next year.” England have also named one potential debutant on the bench in the form of Greg Fisilau, and Borthwick explained what he coud bring to their side. “We’re all absolutely delighted for Greg,” he said. “He’s worked incredibly hard to get to this point and has earned his opportunity through the way he’s performed for Exeter and in our training environment. “He’s a powerful, athletic player who brings real energy to the team.” Kiss was equally as wary of his side’s opposition this weekend, saying: “The entire squad has travelled well and prepared with fantastic energy and excitement heading into this weekend. “Playing England on their home turf – at an iconic venue like Twickenham – is a massive challenge and another great opportunity for us to test ourselves against world-class opposition and keep building our game.” The importance of having Fin Smith coming through this week good to go cannot be overstated for England. The 24-year-old is firmly establishing himself as Borthwick’s go-to fly-half at the moment, with the rest of the attack and the starting backline seemingly built around him. His desire sit just that little bit deeper away from the front line really seems to work within this Lee Blackett system, allowing him to scan across the park and identify space to then send the game breakers through. He is also more than comfortable taking the line on himself and then playing flat to it, which only adds to his game and England’s shape. Want more from Planet Rugby? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for world-class coverage you can trust. Wing duo Immanuel Feyi-Waboso and Tommy Freeman will also likely have a major impact on proceedings. While slightly different types of wingers, they both give England’s attack genuine power and pace, all while floating in and around play to just get their hands on the ball. They are also both supreme finishers when given a sniff of the line, which is crucial at this level. England will also likely lean on number eight Ben Earl to help lay the foundations in the tight. As he has so often proved in pretty much the entirety of Borthwick’s tenure as head coach, Earl is England’s chief battering ram up front with his willingness to carry and ability to break through the gainline almost at will, but he also acts as a key strike option in counter-attack play, as if he’s an extra centre when England are given broken field. His ability to slot into midfield is also a big tick in his box, with Borthwick returning to a 6-2 split on the bench. Australia also come into this one with an exciting wing duo of their own, in the form of Max Jorgensen and Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii. In a similar way to England’s pairing, these two offer a really different set of skills to this Wallaby attack. Jorgensen’s pace makes him a real danger in broken field, while Suaalii’s shift out wide not only sees him given that sort of freedom to float around the pitch and allows Australia to tap into his aerial prowess too. It could have a huge effect on the Wallabies’ attack, if used correctly. Len Ikitau’s return to the side is also a huge boost for Kiss. His injuries have meant we’ve only seen flashes of his quality this year in the Gold jersey, but those have been nothing short of brilliant. He was arguably the best player on the pitch before his knock against the Springboks, and added some nice flicks against Los Pumas as well. His blend of silky handling and genuine grunt in the carry make him an all-round threat, and that should make him a prominent part of the attack this weekend. Ryan Lonergan is also becoming a major player for the Wallabies in their recent run. He just seems to add a real layer of control and calmness to their play from the base of the ruck, almost in that French-style mould, and he should take a lot of the load of new fly-half Declan Meredith in the process. His goal-kicking is also top-notch, which is only a good thing at Test level. Lukhan Salakaia-Loto has been dipped in and out of the side in recent years, but he seems Kiss trusts him to go around and act as their chief enforcer. And it only brings the best out of him. The hulking forward relishes the ugly work in the tight, where he can smash and bash through the opposition. We’re cheating slightly here, but the battle of the back-row units is too good to ignore or pick just one from. It almost seems they perfectly match one another, too. At eight, Harry Wilson and Ben Earl will simply cart around for fun ball-in-hand, acting as their side’s chief ball carriers in the tight and helping set the tone for the rest of their pack in the process. At openside, Fraser McReight and Ben Curry will likely go toe-to-toe in the breakdown as they are tasked with trying to outdo the other and give their team the upper hand along the way. Interestingly, both coaches have opted for a hybrid at blindside, with the Wallabies shifting Jeremy Williams to blindside and Ollie Chessum continuing his back-row run for England too. This is clearly a move that gives them a big bopper to balance things out in that unit to free up their flanking partner, but also adds an extra option at the lineout as well. With the teams matching each other and the back-rows looking almost identical in their making, it will simply come down to whoever wants it more on the day. And that is an even more mouthwatering prospect. There is a lot of chatter, talk, noise, whatever you want to call it, surrounding this Test on Sunday, but England should pass this acid test. Ireland v Argentina: Five takeaways as ‘outstanding’ Hugo Keenan shines to leave ‘harsh truth’ for Felipe Contepomi Look, the noise, chatter, talk (nerves?) are not baseless. Australia are a team on the up once again and on a run of five wins from seven under new boss Kiss, including the scalp of the Springboks in that time. England are back in the winners column themselves, but you feel they need a properly convincing one to push their way back to the top table. And what better time to do that than this weekend, on home soil, in front of a packed-out Allianz Stadium. In the here and now, our money is on England to edge it. England’s selection is built around getting the upper hand in the tight and almost outwrestling the Wallabies. The front-row is built for all-out attack in the scrum, the back-row is pretty heavy metal and the bench is custom-made in the same mould as the unit that blew Australia away a year ago. If they can fire as designed, it does feel like the hosts will have just enough. title: Crystal Palace v Liverpool: Team news - Liverpool FC
content: Andoni Iraola reported no fresh injury concerns ahead of Crystal Palace v Liverpool, though Ryan Gravenberch is a doubt for the trip to Selhurst Park. Midfielder Gravenberch did not travel for Wednesday’s game at Fenerbahce due to the heel problem that also prevented him from playing against Arsenal last weekend. Reds head coach Iraola held his pre-Palace press conference on Friday afternoon and, when asked for a squad fitness update, replied: “The only doubt we will have is Ryan. The others will be the same as we have been. “The Ryan Gravenberch thing is a day-to-day thing, it’s a matter of pain. Let’s see if he can deal with the pain and he can help us.” Sunday’s 2pm GMT kick-off comes too soon for Jeremie Frimpong – who has missed the last five games because of a muscle issue – while Conor Bradley, Hugo Ekitike and Giovanni Leoni are long-term absentees. Bradley Barcola started as Liverpool’s central forward in the midweek Champions League defeat in Istanbul and Iraola was quizzed on the likelihood of the France international being deployed there again this season. “Bradley is a winger. He mostly has played as a left winger, sometimes as a right winger but also has played in PSG as a striker. It’s something that I wanted to try,” the boss said. “I thought against the centre-backs he could be a threat, especially in behind. But he’s a winger and he will be mostly, 90 per cent of the time, used as a winger. But I think it’s alternatives that I sometimes want to try. “I tried with Cody [Gakpo] against Chelsea, I think, in the Carabao Cup and not maybe from the beginning but it’s true that during the games I think it’s options that we can use when Alex [Isak] is tired and we need another type of striker. “We can use other strikers that we have but also wingers that can do a job there.” Andoni Iraola's pre-Crystal Palace press conference Palace, meanwhile, will be without forwards Jean-Philippe Mateta and Ismaila Sarr on Sunday. Mateta is suspended after he was sent off in the Eagles’ loss to Tottenham Hotspur last weekend, while Sarr has not featured in their four most recent matches and will not return until after the November international break, according to manager Pierre Sage. Sage sees Eddie Nketiah and Jorgen Strand Larsen as options to replace Mateta, saying: “As you know, JP [Mateta] was injured at the beginning of the season. “There was the opportunity for Jorgen Strand Larsen and Eddie Nketiah to play. He will miss [the game], but we have to deal with it. We have big confidence in the other players. They’ve shown they are able to play and they are able to compete. “We need them in the play, we need them to press, we need them to score, to finalise the offensive play. Jorgen showed that against Ipswich and against Lech Poznan, that’s why we know he’s able to score. “Eddie scored against Fulham, he scored against Lech Poznan too, and Eddie is able to play as a No. 10 too. “That’s why we will see what will happen on Sunday – but we have some solutions.” Strand Larsen was an unused substitute for Palace’s 1-1 draw with Hoffenheim in the Europa League on Thursday night, following a three-match absence. Sage completed his pre-Liverpool media duties immediately after that game and, on Strand Larsen’s fitness, stated: “He didn’t play today because the scenario of the game was not positive for him to have the possibility to let him play. “But I think he’s able to play 60, 75 [minutes] and with the head and the stamina, maybe he can push this.” 'Now we have to react' - more from Iraola's pre-Palace press conference Crystal Palace 1-1 Hoffenheim (November 5): Henderson, Richards, Canvot, Ahanor, Khalaili, Timber, Wharton, Mitchell, Kamada, Pino, Mateta. Fenerbahce 3-2 Liverpool (November 4): Alisson, Gomez, Jacquet, Van Dijk, Tsimikas, Mac Allister, Nyoni, Munoz, Szoboszlai, Ngumoha, Barcola.

title: Buatsi v Hutchinson 2 - world light-heavyweight title fight predictions - BBC
content: Joshua Buatsi and Willy Hutchinson renew their rivalry for the vacant WBC world light-heavyweight title in Manchester on Saturday. The British rivals first met in a highly entertaining, hard-fought contest on the undercard of Daniel Dubois' win over Anthony Joshua in September 2024. Londoner Buatsi, 33, twice knocked down Hutchinson before going on to win by split decision. Scotland's Hutchinson, 28, suffered the second defeat of his professional career that night but two wins since have put him in a position to fight for a first world title. Can Buatsi repeat his victory? Or will Hutchinson gain revenge in Manchester? BBC Sport spoke to figures from across the boxing world to get their predictions. Hutchinson finding happiness after emotional turmoil "Buatsi may stop him this time in the later rounds. I think he gets it done between rounds nine and 12." "Willy has improved massively since the first fight, whereas I'm not sure I could say the same for Joshua." "It's a really good fight. I think the first fight was very good - Willy was dropped a couple of times in the fight and that cost him. Otherwise, his performance was OK. He's matured a lot since that fight and is in good form. "Buatsi has maybe just started to look old but the fact the world title is on the line... When he turned professional, everyone thought he was a shoo-in to become world champion and he hasn't achieved it yet. This is the chance, so we may see a level of Buatsi that we haven't seen in a while. "I think it'll be really competitive but I'm just edging Hutchinson to win on points with the run of form he's on." "Willy Hutchinson will get the win - it's his time. Buatsi is a tough fighter and it won't be easy but when I look at who is fresh and who has the bit between their teeth a little more - I'm backing Hutchinson." "I'm going for a repeat for Buatsi and he finally gets his hands on a world title. It has been 10 years since he was at the Olympics and it felt like he slipped away from that batch of fighters. "Buatsi does things in his own time and he's finally got his shot. It comes at a great time for him, it could go two ways - he's either overconfident because he's beaten Willy or his confidence could be a good thing and he could step on it early and I think it's the second one. "I can't see Willy getting stopped - he's tough - so I'm going Buatsi on points, but he might get a knockdown." "It's very rare people can turn the rematch around when they lose the first one. On that basis, I am going for Joshua Buatsi, possibly even by late stoppage." "I'm going with Buatsi to win again. Hutchinson showed he was weak to the body and that could be his kryptonite. "Hutchinson is a good fighter; he's slick and sharp, but I think Buatsi has his number and wins on points." "Willy Hutchinson is in his physical and mental prime and I think he wins the fight. I've known Willy since he turned professional as an 18-year-old. "He's always had the tools to be a world champion and I believe timing is everything in boxing. I believe he's also catching Buatsi at the right time." "What a rematch. He showed his worth, his bottle and his ability did Willy Hutchinson in that first fight and proved a lot as a fighter. "Joshua Buatsi had a very good fight with Callum Smith, although he came out second best. Not so impressive in his win over Zach Parker, it was a close fight so a lot of questions surround him and what's left. "Hutchinson is a man in form and looks like a man who is matured both physically and mentally. This is a fantastic rematch with the WBC light-heavyweight title on the line. It promises to be an action-packed contest and the pot of gold is massive." "A rematch that I didn't think would come around but it all makes sense with the added incentive of gold. Someone will leave as world champion. The first time they fought, it was 80-20 Buatsi for me, but Hutchinson was a lot better than I expected. "He has now closed that gap drastically and now it's 55-45 Buatsi. How much has Callum Smith taken out of Buatsi? On the flip side, Hutchinson, after that defeat, has gone from strength to strength. "He showed everything in his last fight against Ezra Taylor. I favour Buatsi just, but we'll see how much that Smith fight took out of him. I think Buatsi will be world champion, but I wouldn't be surprised if Willy Hutchinson walks home with gold." title: Ireland v Argentina: Winners and losers as Irish stars showcase 'remarkable rugby IQ' while Shaun Edwards has 'inauspicious' start - Planet Rugby
content: Ireland's hat-trick hero against Argentina, Hugo Keenan, and new Los Pumas defence coach Shaun Edwards. Following a 42-12 victory for Ireland over Argentina at the Aviva Stadium in Dublin on Friday, here are our winners and losers from the Nations Championship clash. The hat-trick hero for the hosts but his performance was much more than that. Keenan obviously showed great try-scoring instincts and quality to cross the whitewash three times, but he was also exceptional elsewhere. He has remarkable rugby IQ and always positions himself superbly in backfield while his hands are solid on the kick receipt and his one-on-one tackling is among the best around. A truly world-class player who never lets Ireland down. One of Los Pumas’ few standouts. Scored both of his side’s tries and never stopped working as he constantly got his hands on the ball and made ground. Both of Carreras’ finishes were superb as he displayed his vast array of skills to at least give something for his supporters to smile about. Considering his small stature, the wing is incredibly strong in contact and difficult to bring to ground but, unfortunately for the visitors, he was pretty much their only threat. There were glimpses from the likes of Santiago Chocobares and Tomas Albornoz, but not much else from the rest. Granted, there were a couple of poor choices from the fly-half, particularly early on, but this was so much better from Prendergast. In fact, his start to the season in general has been good and the subtle changes in his game have paid dividends. Previously, the playmaker was simply standing and delivering – taking the ball stood still and shipping it onto a team-mate – but this season he has been moving onto the pass from his scrum-half. That automatically makes Prendergast a much greater threat and on Friday it enabled him to get the Irish attack moving. He has worked so hard to get himself in a position to be a regular in the Ireland 23 and he more than justified his start with a fine display. Timoney was incredibly busy on both sides of the ball, making ground in the carry and dominating physically in defence. The openside is 31 now but he is enjoying his time in the sun. Ireland player ratings: ‘Simply brilliant’ hat-trick hero the standout but ‘transformative night’ for Sam Prendergast and some ‘robust’ forwards Another player to make a big difference to this Irish side is Hansen. He has endured his injury troubles but when fit the wing adds so much to the team. Like Keenan, he has an exceptional rugby brain and his ability to inject himself at just the right time is very impressive, while his skill level allows him to execute when he gets in those good positions. There has been criticism of Ireland’s attack since the end of the 2023 Rugby World Cup. New Zealander Goodman took over from Mike Catt in 2024, but the free-flowing and clinical style which became synonymous with the Irish has been absent a bit too often over the past couple of years. However, there has been glimpses in 2026, including a couple of superb performances against England and Scotland in the Six Nations, and this effort was just as promising. They lost their rhythm late on but for 55 minutes this was like the Ireland of old. Joined last month on a deal until the end of the 2027 Rugby World Cup and on this evidence he has plenty of work to do. Either that or Edwards has indeed lost his magic touch as a defence coach after France started leaking points under his stewardship. Ireland v Argentina: Five takeaways as ‘outstanding’ Hugo Keenan shines to leave ‘harsh truth’ for Felipe Contepomi After a bright start from the South Americans, holes started to appear as the Irish brilliantly manipulated the visiting rearguard to touch down six times in the opening hour. Certainly not the most auspicious start to Edwards’ stint. While Los Pumas weren’t particularly great in defence, it did not help that they could not set a platform in the set-piece. Quite simply the lineout was abysmal with Julian Montoya having a very poor day at the office before he was replaced following a head injury. Leonel Oviedo then came on for Montoya and it did not get much better with the replacement also struggling. He then also suffered a HIA with prop Boris Wenger briefly taking over throwing responsibilities, and it says a lot that he arguably did a better job. Oviedo did return to put in an improve showing but the damage had been done on the scoreboard by that point. Although the hookers may bear the brunt of the criticism for Argentina’s set-piece fallibility, the back five of the scrum, and especially the second-row, should also not be excused. Pedro Rubiolo in particular had a shocker, and not just for their struggles in the set-piece. Rubiolo attempted 14 tackles and missed six of them in what was a poor day for the pack. Want more from Planet Rugby? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for world-class coverage you can trust. Speaking of missed tackles, Kremer was awry with five attempts – second behind Rubiolo – in what was a surprisingly poor performance from the top-class forward. Usually so abrasive and the standard-setter at close quarters, he was bullied by Ireland and failed to reach the level required. Los Pumas did stem the bleeding in the latter stages of the contest, but it felt like it was more a case of Ireland reducing the intensity when the game was won than anything the Argentinians did. Efrain Elias summed up their woes by getting sin-binned just a few minutes after coming on as the replacements never managed to alter the momentum. It was a terrible all-round showing from Felipe Contepomi’s men. title: Greene v. Google LLC - Loeb & Loeb LLP
content:
California state court upholds radio and podcast host David Greene’s right of publicity, misappropriation, unfair competition and unjust enrichment claims alleging that Google’s use of his voice as the default male voice for its NotebookLM product and in related marketing constituted unlawful use of his “voice” in violation of California’s statutory and common law right of publicity laws, and that the claims are not preempted by the Copyright Act. Plaintiff David Greene, who hosted NPR’s Morning Edition and the podcast Up First and currently hosts the podcast Left, Right & Center, sued Google LLC and its parent, Alphabet Inc., asserting California state law claims related to Google’s use of recordings of his voice to create the default male voice for the “Audio Overviews” feature of its NotebookLM product, and Google’s use of that voice to market and sell the product, without his permission. Google’s Audio Overviews, introduced in September 2024, turn uploaded documents into a podcast-like conversation between two AI “hosts,” one male and one female. Greene alleged that Google trained its model on his voice or recordings of it and that the male host in NotebookLM renders text into speech “calibrated to replicate Mr. Greene’s unique vocal qualities, cadence, tone, pitch, and expressive style.” In the alternative, he alleged that “regardless of the precise technical means used,” Google deliberately made the male host sound so much like him that ordinary listeners believed the voice was his. Greene asserted four causes of action: (1) statutory right of publicity under California Civil Code Section 3344, (2) unfair competition under California Business and Professions Code Section 17200, (3) common law right of publicity and (4) unjust enrichment/quasi-contract. Google removed the case to federal court on a complete preemption theory, but the Northern District of California concluded that the claims fall outside copyright’s subject matter, because a person’s voice and identity are not copyrightable. (Read our summary of the district court’s decision here.) After the case was remanded to state court, Google demurred to all four claims, arguing that Section 3344 does not apply to an AI-generated voice that merely resembles Greene’s, that the complaint fails to state any claim, that the Copyright Act preempts every claim and that Alphabet is not a proper defendant. The court overruled Google’s demurrer to every cause of action but sustained Alphabet’s demurrer with leave to amend. The court first turned to whether Greene adequately alleged that the use of his voice stated a claim under Section 3344. The court rejected defendants’ argument based on Midler v. Ford Motor Co., in which the Ninth Circuit held that the statute was “of no aid” to Bette Midler because the sound-alike singer Ford hired used another singer’s voice, not Midler’s. The court distinguished Midler, explaining that Greene’s complaint alleges that Google trained its voice model on recordings of Greene’s own voice, adjusted its output to duplicate his voice and generated a voice that is “unquestionably Mr. Greene’s voice.” According to the court, “the output is not someone else’s voice that happens to resemble Greene’s. It is a digital rendering of Greene’s voice created from Greene’s voice.” The court found support in the text of Section 3344, which covers the knowing use of another’s “voice ... in any manner” and does not limit “voice” to a particular unmodified recording. The court held that this text provided no reason to distinguish a digital reproduction of a voice generated from recordings of that voice from a reproduction of a person’s image, which triggers Section 3344.
The court also rejected defendants’ argument that the California legislature’s treatment of “digital replicas” shows that Section 3344 excludes them. The court took judicial notice of SB 1111, which the California governor signed on Sept. 30, 2026, and which adds a new subdivision (f) to Section 3344, providing that “a voice or likeness includes a digital replica.” The court further held that Greene adequately pleaded a direct connection between the unauthorized use and Google’s commercial purpose in order to state a claim under Section 3344. It explained that Greene was not required to plead specific facts showing that his identity was a substantial factor in sales. Instead, the claim applies to uses “on or in products” and to uses “for purposes of advertising or selling.” The court held that Greene’s complaint alleges both uses by alleging that his voice is the default male host in a subscription product, that Google chose it “to create familiarity for seasoned podcast listeners and, in effect, maximize Google’s profits,” and that Google used Greene’s voice in demonstrations, promotional materials and a Spotify partnership promoting NotebookLM. Turning to the common law misappropriation claim, the court noted that the elements are (1) the defendant’s use of the plaintiff’s identity; (2) the appropriation of the plaintiff’s name or likeness to the defendant’s advantage, commercially or otherwise; (3) lack of consent; and (4) resulting injury. As to the first prong, defendants argued that Greene was required to plead facts showing that his voice is distinctive and widely known, that Google deliberately imitated it to sell a product and that people familiar with his voice believed Greene himself performed the AI output. The court rejected the last of these as a pleading element but held that Greene satisfied the first three. The court held that Greene adequately alleged that his voice was distinctive and well-known, because a radio host “reaches the audience through the voice.” As to deliberate imitation, the court relied on allegations that Google chose Greene’s voice to create familiarity for podcast listeners, built the voice from his recordings, calibrated it to replicate his vocal traits and knew he was recognizable. The court likewise held that Greene adequately pleaded appropriation of his voice to Google’s advantage. The court rejected Google’s reliance on federal AI training decisions that require plaintiffs to identify the specific works used to train a model. The common law tort does not, the court explained, turn on training but instead requires only deliberate imitation of a distinctive voice to sell a product. The court similarly found the complaint’s allegations that Google uses Greene’s voice as a default host in a paid product, in promotions and in a commercial partnership sufficient to allege Google’s advantage. The court similarly held that Greene pleaded resulting injury by alleging that Google usurped the market value of his voice and that the false association with NotebookLM has reduced the value of his voice as a licensable asset, impaired his ability to license it to others and produced AI-generated podcasts that compete with his work. Turning to Greene’s unfair competition claim, the court first held that Greene had standing because the alleged diminution of the commercial value of Greene’s identity, which California treats as a property interest, is a cognizable economic injury. Greene also pleaded unlawful conduct through the “predicate” violation of Section 3344. The court similarly upheld Greene’s unjust enrichment claim as a quasi-contract claim for restitution. It held that Greene’s allegations of Google’s use of the commercial value of his voice to develop, promote and sell NotebookLM without consent or payment adequately pleaded that Google unjustly retained a benefit. The court next considered Google’s assertion of copyright preemption as to all four claims. The two-part copyright preemption test asks (1) whether the subject matter of the state law claim falls within the subject matter of the Copyright Act and (2) whether the rights asserted under state law are equivalent to the exclusive rights under 17 U.S.C. Section 106. Both elements must be satisfied for preemption to apply. The court held that copyright preemption did not apply because Greene’s claims rest upon the alleged appropriation of his voice and identity, neither of which is copyrightable. Agreeing with the federal court that had previously held preemption inapplicable in its remand order, the state court noted that Greene’s claims are “fundamentally about the program’s outputs,” not its inputs. The court reasoned that Greene alleges not that Google reproduced or distributed his recordings but rather that it generated new speech in his voice that he never recorded. Copyright would not reach that conduct, the court noted, “even if Greene owned every recording he made,” since a sound-recording copyright does not extend to independent sounds that imitate the recording. The court acknowledged that any theory treating the copying of Greene’s recordings as independently actionable under state law may be preempted. However, because each cause of action Greene asserted rested on the appropriation of his voice and identity, which were not copyrightable, the court declined to dismiss all claims on preemption grounds. Finally, the court turned to Alphabet’s argument that the complaint failed to state a basis for holding it responsible as Google’s alter ego. The court agreed, holding that the complaint’s alter ego and agency allegations were conclusory. The complaint lacked any facts showing that honoring Google’s separate existence would promote injustice or that Alphabet participated in developing, training, deploying or promoting the male host’s voice, the court explained. The court accordingly dismissed all claims as to Alphabet with leave to amend. title: Ireland player ratings v Argentina: Hugo Keenan impresses in hat-trick display - The Irish Times
content: Ran an intelligent support line for his first, brilliant footwork for his second, a run-in for his third, aerially competitive, chased, harried and tackled, while covering the backfield with an impressive vigilance. Rating: 9 It was his arcing break that led to Ireland’s first try and he looked lethal in possession. Pace kills. Won some aerial duels too in an excellent all-round effort. His work in defence is occasionally overlooked but it should not be the case. Rating: 8 Unfussy and diligent in his work-rate he carried when his team needed and in defence was disciplined in jockeying at times and not biting in on the tackle. One or two nicely timed passes. Rating: 7 A couple of passes that were a little shy on the trajectory and pace, but he occupied the Pumas midfield and did carry well on occasion requiring more than one defender to stop him. A quieter outing by his lofty standards. Rating: 6 Given his absence from Test rugby through injury there was always going to be an acclimatisation process. Conceded an early penalty and snatched at a kick but his work for the first try and ability to occupy tacklers provided space for others was super. Grew into the game. Rating: 7 Bright opening, nice wrap on Ireland’s first try, kicked away a bit of ball, decisions he might like to have over again, but had numerous touches of class in both kicking and distribution. His try was a delight. Took the licks to let team-mates prosper. Rating: 8 Caught on cross-kick defending in the wide channel for Mateo Carreras try having twice called for backup. Sharp and alive in his work, his kicking was excellent, in a fine display. Rating: 8 Won a scrum penalty, carried through tacklers that gave his team front-foot ball and also occupied multiple defenders, intelligently looking for the pace between them. Nice mix to his work and got a late cameo at tighthead. Rating: 7 Involved multiple times for his try, throw, carry and pass, and then the act of dotting down. Superb in the loose, beating tackles with footwork and power before failing to return from a Head Injury Assessment. Rating: 7 Superb penalty turnover when Ireland were under serious pressure near their own line, he was another whose no nonsense carrying gave his team go-forward ball and made his tackles. Scrum went well too. Rating: 7 Good carry through traffic, his footwork into contact and lines of running was first class, while he was also a one-man maul wrecking machine. Another high-quality display. Rating: 8 Elected to carry when possession was slow and was typically difficult to shift when slowing down Argentina ruck ball and filching the odd one. Rating: 8 Beaten on the outside with a fend on a Pumas counterattack but thereafter his quality in the lineout caused Argentina huge problems, from pinching the ball outright to forcing crooked throws. Good overhead pass for Keenan hat-trick. Rating: 7 His clever feet for Sheehan’s try was a classic example of what he brings in the carrying game, so too his tackling when snuffing out visiting attacks. Rating: 7 Straight and hard in his running, took his lumps in two-man tackles without dialling down his commitment to the cause. Limped off early in the second half. Rating: 6 Rónan Kelleher was a first-half replacement and try scorer. Ciarán Frawley was lively. There were one or two other decent individual moments for those that came on but without quite making the anticipated impact. There’s an argument that the Argentina bench provided a little more impetus. Rating: 6 Andy Farrell will be pleased with the result, large tranches of the performance for a first outing since the summer and with the cohesion shown for the most part. His faith in rewarding a few players was repaid. Rating: 7 Join our dedicated Rugby WhatsApp channel for all the action What’s making headlines in the rugby world? content: Democrat James Talarico won a Senate seat in Texas, breaking a 38-year drought for his party in the Republican stronghold and delivering a stunning blow to Donald Trump.
