title: Hamilton v Leclerc: how can Ferrari solve problem of two number one drivers? - The Guardian
content: The Scuderia are hopeful of being in the world championship mix next season but risk puncturing their chances if they can’t corral their men in the cockpits Going into this weekend’s São Paulo Grand Prix, all indications are that the status quo at Ferrari will no longer suffice for Lewis Hamilton if the Scuderia’s ambition to return their first drivers’ Formula One championship since 2007 is to be taken seriously. This year’s drivers’ title is already decided with Kimi Antonelli triumphant at the last round in Mexico and Ferrari are looking towards next season where they are hopeful of genuinely being in the mix against the Italian and Mercedes. However, after Hamilton and his teammate Charles Leclerc clashed at the Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez, the Briton clearly believes that a title tilt in 2027 might be at risk, as the team apparently vacillate on how to manage having two No 1 drivers, both determined to be the top dog around which Ferrari should coalesce. In Mexico, with Leclerc attempting to pass Hamilton, the move cost them both, Leclerc with a penalty and Hamilton in going wide and being passed by Max Verstappen who went on to win. The outcome denied Ferrari what would have been a likely victory and potentially a one-two. The team principal, Fred Vasseur, condemned the incident as demonstrating a lack of respect for the team and was expected to hold a crunch meeting with them both at Interlagos on Friday. It was not the first time this season the two Ferrari drivers have been uncompromising with one another. At Zandvoort Hamilton was frustrated when, on a different tyre strategy, Leclerc did not pit when first instructed to do so by the team in order to let the British driver past. A race later at Monza, Hamilton went down the inside of Leclerc into the first chicane and was squeezed wide by his teammate into the gravel. The notable difference after Mexico was Hamilton’s reaction. Previously he has been politic in stating they would deal with incidents behind closed doors – “offline” as he refers to it. After Mexico he publicly criticised Leclerc and before the race in Brazil was more bullish, refusing to be silenced in his criticism and making his position clear. “Naturally it’s not so easy having someone like me come into a team because I’m very outspoken,” he said. “I push and push and push for so many changes and I’m going to be pushing for more and as long as I’m here that’s how it’s going to be. I’m here to win.” That he is talking about it publicly indicates the seriousness of the situation. The team have no formal rules of engagement between the two and pointedly neither is considered the top driver in the way that Verstappen is at Red Bull. Last year with the team struggling it was irrelevant. This year the problem has been brought sharply into focus. With a title at stake in the future it could be the difference between winning and losing but this is far from a straightforward situation. Hamilton came to Ferrari on the back of enjoying de facto No 1 status at Mercedes, pretty much since Nico Rosberg retired after thein 2016 season. Leclerc, who is no less competitive, has enjoyed similar pre-eminence at Ferrari, with whom he has forged a strong relationship since he joined in 2019 and was long the favoured choice as their expected next champion. The complex demands and the fallout from letting them battle for dominance is far from new, as seen with Ayrton Senna and Alain Prost and Nigel Mansell and Nelson Piquet. Hamilton also knows about it, not least after his acrimonious fight with Rosberg in 2016. The latter was such that Mercedes, having been at pains to allow their drivers to race, had to impose rules of engagement. Vasseur has been painstaking so far in avoiding that scenario but he was left enormously frustrated after the incident in Mexico and knows how costly it could be. His is a very delicate balancing act however. McLaren had a similar problem with Oscar Piastri and Lando Norris in 2024 and 2025, and their efforts to allow their drivers to race without favour but also in managing them to the team’s advantage led to the adoption of their torturously complex “papaya rules”. These were satisfying to neither drivers nor fans, and did not appear particularly edifying to the team themselves. Notably however they did come out of it with the constructors’ title in 2024 and the double in 2025, a result that will not be lost on Ferrari. It has largely not been a problem for McLaren this season, with Norris enjoying a distinct advantage over his Australian teammate, of which Hamilton and Leclerc are aware. Both are determined to make themselves the focal point of the team; both are aware how important that is if the title is at stake. This has led to another fundamental problem for Ferrari. By not intervening in the process, they have seen the trust between the pair seemingly stretched to breaking point. Perhaps, it feels, within a whisker of becoming actively counterproductive from which a further, more damaging deterioration threatens. As Hamilton appears to be now insisting, Ferrari must address the issue but Leclerc cannot be faulted for simply following his instincts as a competitor. Both drivers are committed to the team but both are as equally determined to win, ambitions that match those of the Scuderia, which if they are to be met they must surely now look to manage. In first practice at Interlagos, McLaren’s Norris topped the timesheets in front of the new champion Antonelli in second, with Verstappen third and Hamilton fourth. In the afternoon Antonelli was on top, from Norris and Verstappen with Mercedes’ George Russell in fourth. Russell is, however, set to take a five-place grid penalty on Sunday for using a new engine in Brazil. Hamilton and Leclerc were in sixth and seventh.

title: We Took a Cadillac XLR-V Onto Europe’s Most Challenging Roads, and It Delivered - MotorTrend
content: We tackled some of Europe’s fastest and most challenging roads in a Cadillac. [This story originally appeared in the January 2008 issue of Motor Trend with the headline "A Long Way From Motown," and comes from a time when we had a space in our name.] The Porsches don’t want to play. Over 1000 hard-charging miles in two days across Germany, Austria, and Italy, and not one appears in the Cadillac’s sights. Which is a pity, because our wedgy, quad-piped XLR-V is locked and loaded for 911s. Whoa! Back up a minute! Did I just say we went chasing Porsches … in a Cadillac? In Germany? Um, yeah. Because that’s exactly what we did. And while the 911s proved elusive, no one—apart from a lunatic in a black BMW 645i convertible who kept the hammer down in a speed-limited construction zone—passed our XLR-V on the autobahnen. Not the silver-haired guy in the big, black Audi S8 with Wuppertal plates. Nor the guy in the E46 M3 who tried to run with us near Nuremberg. Nor even the guy in the AMG Benz who gave us a cold, hard stare after we blew by him near Mainz. They couldn’t keep up. Cadillac general manager Jim Taylor clearly has a sense of adventure, because when I idly suggested a while back it might be fun to disable the 155-mph speed limiter on an XLR-V and take it to Germany to see what it would do on highways with no speed limits, he didn’t suddenly look at his watch and start mumbling something about a meeting he had to catch. Instead, he simply cracked a wry grin: “That sounds like fun. Let me see what I can do.” Third gear is stunning, giving you an effective operating range of 37 to 129 mph. Lord only knows what it took to shepherd the idea through GM; every few months I’d see Taylor at some event or other and he’d always say, “I haven’t forgotten.” But Cadillac’s decision to hold preview drives of the all-new CTS sedan at the Nürburgring made a bunch of logistics a whole lot easier, which is how photographer Mark Bramley and I came to be pulling out of the car park of the Hyatt Regency Hotel in Mainz, Germany, bound for Italy and the famed Stelvio Pass in an Infrared metallic XLR-V. Why the Stelvio Pass? Well, as British mountaineer George Leigh Mallory explained when asked in 1923 why he wanted to climb Mt. Everest: “Because it’s there.” Located where Switzerland kisses Italy and Austria, the 9045-foot Stelvio is the second-highest paved pass in the Alps. Originally built in the 1820s, and little changed since, it reaches a one-in-nine gradient at some points and features 48 hairpins on the northern side. The view of the road writhing down the ancient glacial valley is one of the most iconic in motoring. “Our” XLR-V was stock apart from a simple change to the engine-management computer that banished the speed nanny to the electronic ether. GM also took the precaution of X-raying the wheels and tires for any cracks or faults, though if you think about it, you’re not going to be in that much more trouble if a tire pops at 170 mph or so than if it does at the regulation 155. Still, it’s nice to know they care. Contrary to popular legend, Germany’s autobahnen aren’t pedal-to-the-metal paradises where you can run as fast as you dare, as long as you like. Germany is slightly smaller than Montana, but has a population of more than 80 million people. So many of the country’s superhighways often look like rush hour in L.A., clogged with slow-moving cars and trucks. The natural gait of the XLR-V is somewhere between 135 and 140 mph. We take the long way out of Mainz to avoid the worst of the congestion, driving west, then south, before swinging east to cross the Rhine and head toward Heidelberg. Just as we turn east, where the A61 meets the A6, we bust the second autobahn myth: There are speed limits, and they’re ruthlessly enforced. Wheeling around a long on-ramp, something flashes in my peripheral vision, and as we clear the corner there’s a German police car, blue lights flashing along with a “Follow Me” sign—helpfully in English and French, as well as in German. He leads us into a nearby rest area where we join an orderly line of fellow drivers, licenses and wallets in hand, standing outside a Mercedes van. A guardrail-mounted speed camera has nailed the XLR-V at 80 mph in a 60 zone. As we wait, Bramley says Germany’s started to crack down hard on speeding drivers and warns me this could be expensive. As it turns out, there’s a sliding scale of fines, and foreigners get off a lot more lightly than do Germans. The cop relieves me of 95 euro—about $130. “For you, it’s cheap,” he smiles. Transaction over, we walk back to the car. I’m just about to fire up the supercharged V-8 when I see the cop striding toward us. Uh-oh, here comes the lecture. I roll down the window. The cop reaches into his pocket, pulls out a packet of cigarettes, and eyes the Michigan-plated Caddy, the brash Yank on a European vacation. Suddenly, he grins: “Now, I must say this: Gentlemen, start your engines!” Then he throws back his head, and roars with laughter. A German traffic cop with a sense of humor. Now I’ve seen everything. Back on the road, and clear of speed limits, we loaf along at 100 mph or so until the traffic clears and I can nail the gas. There’s a momentary lull as the six-speed auto shuffles back a couple ratios, then the Northstar growls into action. I see 168 mph on the head-up display (the speedo runs only to 160) before the traffic builds again, and I’m forced to back off. Analog speedo tops out at 160 mph, but we saw 171 mph on the head-up digital display. We cruise as fast as the traffic allows down to the Austrian border. The XLR-V’s natural gait is somewhere between 135 and 140 mph—a relatively restrained 2800 to 3000 rpm in the moonshot sixth gear. At these speeds it feels as comfortable, relaxed, and stable as an SL, though there’s much more wind noise from around the roof than in the Mercedes. Bramley no stranger to fast and exotic European machinery, raises an approving eyebrow. “It’s better than I thought it would be,” he says. The Cadillac is far from a Benz rival in other ways, though—you need only one glance around the cabin, taking in the cheap-looking plastics, old-school switchgear, and low-rent graphics to see that. The ergonomics could be better, too: The seat cushion is too short, and the pedals too high and vertical. You’d never guess GM once led the world in the study of biomechanics. It’s late afternoon by the time we reach Italy and the north side of the Stelvio. The XLR-V has proven surprisingly quick and agile on the smooth mountain roads, reminding me a lot—and, yes, I’m surprised to find myself writing this—of our Jaguar XKR long-termer. The Cadillac has that same fast yet relaxed feel of the Jag, although the British car steers more crisply, rides better, brakes harder, and feels much more rigidly constructed. Still, there’s the genesis of a great GT in this Cadillac. All GM has to do is sweat the details. The 443-horsepower, supercharged Northstar V-8 is a gem, smooth and flexible and willing to rev, with a solid side order of torque on hand whenever you need it. I move the shift lever across the gate into manual mode, working through second, third, and fourth as we zigzag through the hills. Third gear is stunning—the V-8 pulls like a train from 2000 rpm and doesn’t stop until it nudges 6700, giving you an effective operating range of 37 to 129 mph. The Caddy demolishes short straightaways and barely draws breath up the hills, the V-8 exhaust note booming off the rock walls. The Stelvio itself is astonishing. The road climbs steadily through the forest, switchbacks here and there, before we break through the treeline. Then the hairpins pile one on top of the other; in places the road doubles back on itself two or three times in the space of a few hundred yards. Traffic’s light—most of the bikers who swarm over the place on summer weekends are already in their hotels enjoying an early evening beer—so I can push a little, punching hard out of the hairpins in first gear, snick-snicking into second, then third, before getting hard on the brakes, and double-pumping the shift lever to grab first again for another hairpin. Even with power steering and no clutch pedal, climbing the Stelvio is a physical business. We check into one of the hotels at the very top of the pass. Just down the hill, on the southern side, is the Swiss border. We drive down and cross over, just for the hell of it: It’s not often you get to drive through four countries in one day. Especially in a Cadillac. The next morning dawns bright and clear, so we’re up before breakfast, working the photo ops on the north side of the pass. By the time we finish, it’s past 9 a.m., and Bramley’s due on a 6 p.m. plane out of Frankfurt, more than 500 miles away. I look at the maps and decide we’ll cut east to pick up the autostrada at Merano and drive south to join the A22, which will take us up and over the Brenner Pass back into Austria. It’s going to be a hard slog. The XLR-V draws lots of stares from the car-savvy Italians as we stalk through the shoals of Fiats and Fords on the Brenner Pass. Cadillac’s distinctive visual signature—confident, powerful, chiseled—stands out among the Euro-chic background noise. As with the mechanical package, there’s a world-beating car lurking here, but GM needs to improve panel fit and paint finish (I’ve seen runs along the edge of an XLR-V hood) and finesse the jewelry. The traffic’s heavy, but flowing briskly, and the run down from the top of the Brenner Pass toward Innsbruck gives us the best gas mileage of the trip, 20.5 mpg at an average of 61 mph. But our hopes of making good time to Frankfurt are dashed by a traffic jam just inside the German border, south of Munich. I check the sat nav to find a back road off the autobahn at the next exit, but by the time we wind through a host of picturesque villages and get back onto the A8, we’ve probably burned an hour. We skirt around the east side of Munich and head north, back toward Nuremberg. The traffic clears, and we can run 125-130 mph for a bit. But only a bit—one minute the trip computer says we have 40 miles’ worth of gas left, next we’re running on fumes. I soft-pedal it into a gas station near Nuremberg and pump 15.8 gallons into the tank. We’re struggling to get much more than 250 miles between fuel stops. Memo, Cadillac: A 20-gallon tank would be nice. We make Frankfurt just in time, and I head back to Mainz after dropping Bramley at Departures, looping around to get to a quiet autobahn on the other side of the city. I’m still looking for Porsches. And room to top 168 mph. The A63 is near empty, and unrestricted. Perfect. I settle back in the seat and nail the gas. The Northstar growls, the induction roar ratcheting up an octave as the tach needle swings past 3600 rpm. First gear runs to 47 mph, second to 80, third 124, and fourth hits 165. The transmission slips into fifth, and the digital display keeps ticking off the increments, more slowly now. 169…170…171 mph. And that’s it, not the least because I’ve just chewed through a quarter tank of gas in less than 15 minutes, and I have to find a gas station again. Okay, I didn’t get to surprise any 911s. But I did learn one thing: There’s no reason why Cadillac can’t build a world-beating GT. The XLR-V’s far from perfect, but it’s a lot more at home in Europe than you might think. title: Trumpfall - The Bulwark
content: I was wondering which would break first, Trump’s spirit or his body. The president is an old man. He tries to cover up that fact with hair dye, elaborate combovers, layers of makeup, and other visual f/x. But he’s obviously unwell. Morbidly obese. He falls asleep sitting in public, in meetings, while on camera. His body emits random noises that his underlings pretend not to notice. His voice is weak and strained. His extremities are mottled and swollen. And yet until this week Trump’s spirit had still been strong. His will-to-power intact. His urge to dominate and ability to take the initiative had dulled, but were extant. Since Monday it’s different. We may have broken his back, once and for all. title: Verdict: Is the Acura ADX Just a Luxurious Honda HR-V? Yes, but That’s a Good Thing - MotorTrend
content: Acura builds a surprisingly satisfying luxury experience on a mainstream foundation. Dreams often clash with reality. Indulging in a luxury vehicle can bring style, performance, refinement, and—perhaps most important—the pride of knowing you’ve made it, that you got something better than a simple transportation appliance. At the same time, it can introduce practical perils. Think uncertain reliability, fussy interfaces, and design that compromises function for form. Over 13 months spent driving our yearlong review 2025 Acura ADX, our Acura succeeded in balancing those considerations. How it manages that balancing act will appeal greatly to some drivers and make others steer away. Here’s the rub: The ADX is just so similar to the Honda HR-V. Their dimensions, hardware, interior, features, and even paint are very alike, if not identical. Acuras always use Honda parts but typically try at least a little harder to hide those under a premium veneer. Few subcompact luxury SUV rivals share so much with a mainstream vehicle. That’s a valid concern for drivers who seek badge cachet and want their vehicle to project status in traffic. But otherwise? Not a problem, in my opinion. Honda builds practical, sensible, reliable vehicles with strong value. They tend to drive nicely, too. With that, the HR-V appeals as a normal little crossover that’s easy to use and live with. If that’s the baseline need but there’s a desire for something nicer, something more, then the ADX could be just the thing. Think of it like a luxury trim package for the HR-V, and the ADX starts to make sense. I held that frame of reference during my time with the ADX, and in that, I remained satisfied. The ADX made an adept daily driver. It’s small and easy to park, yet it’s spacious enough to fit my extra-tall self and, with the second-row seats folded, my accordingly tall custom-made bicycle without removing the wheels. It has a bunch of real buttons, which are shared with the HR-V but actuate with a nice tactile feel. In a time when fussy digital controls infest so many cars, these easy-to-use manual knobs and air vents felt like luxury in themselves. Likewise, the familiarity of unlocking with a key, pushing the starter, throwing the shifter into drive, and heading off shouldn’t be underestimated these days. This relative simplicity invites comparison to the HR-V; none of it is particularly high-tech or design-forward. Yet our high-end A-Spec model with the Advance package had touches that elevate it from its Honda basis. The off-white Orchid perforated leather with blue microsuede accents made an appealing combination, and the light upholstery resisted discoloration. The heated and ventilated front seats and heated steering wheel got plenty warm and cool. (More details in our 2025 Acura ADX interior review.) A button on the turn signal stalk activated the 360-degree camera, which became indispensable when parking and maneuvering in tight spaces. The 15-speaker Bang & Olufsen audio system sounds really good, too. For tech, the ADX borrows from the Honda parts bin. Its 10.2-inch digital gauge display looks fine and displays necessary information, but it lacks the reconfigurability and cool graphics seen in some rivals. Likewise, the 9.0-inch infotainment touchscreen had a straightforward user interface, but it’s neither as sharp nor as large as those in competitors. That said, the addition of the Google Gemini AI voice assistant midway through the loan proved to be a useful upgrade. Overall, it’s enough tech but might not impress those who equate huge screens with luxury. The ADX’s reliability and dependability upheld its maker’s reputation. It had no unexpected issues or faults whatsoever. The one scheduled service visit at about 11,000 miles included basics such as an oil change, tire rotation, and inspection of various systems. Although we paid out of pocket due to a stipulation of how Acura allocates test vehicles to media, actual Acura buyers get scheduled maintenance covered during the first 12 months or 12,000 miles of ownership. Beyond that period, owners might anticipate paying the $430.24 we did. Over the 18,652 miles we drove, the ADX averaged 25.4 mpg, reasonably close to its 27-mpg EPA combined fuel economy rating. Cost per mile came to $0.23, reasonable in the context of today’s egregious gas prices; a hybrid ADX would be a welcome addition. The closest comparison from our long-term fleet would be the 2022 Toyota Corolla Cross, another subcompact SUV, which itself underpins a luxury vehicle, the rival Lexus UX. Over its nearly 17,000-mile service life, the Corolla Cross got 29.0 mpg average at a cost per mile of $0.17. Our recently departed 2025 Acura Integra Type S also has a turbocharged I-4 engine and averaged 23.6 mpg at $0.23 per mile over 15,400 miles, not bad considering how hard we drove it. One fueling foible relates to the ADX’s gas tank size. Even though driving range is rated at 378 miles, the most we ever got from a tank was 345 miles—20 miles past the vehicle displaying zero range remaining. Oddly, the fuel gauge shows empty when there are actually two gallons left in the tank, an unnecessarily large buffer. On the plus side, the capless fuel filler is a nice convenience. Some things about the ADX irked me. Wireless Apple CarPlay connectivity was spotty; it usually connected instantly, but occasionally I’d need to select my iPhone from the touchscreen. However, after Gemini and its upgraded Google Maps capability arrived, I basically stopped using CarPlay. The passenger-side mirror tilts down in reverse but wouldn’t always rise back up to exactly where I’d set it. Most annoying was the terrible adaptive cruise control. It was extremely slow to respond to traffic ahead, sometimes taking several seconds to detect a braking vehicle. I’d see taillights illuminate then count to three or four before it reacted abruptly. This feature works better in every other Acura and Honda I’ve tried, making its application in our ADX seem like an unfortunate fluke. Whenever I drove myself, though, I enjoyed the ADX’s connected dynamics. Its 190-hp, 179 lb-ft 1.5-liter turbocharged I-4 and CVT automatic produced an objectively slow-for-its-segment 8.9-second 0–60-mph time, and wide-open acceleration was accompanied by a coarse soundtrack. But that was rarely needed. Torque arrives promptly, making the little engine feel stronger than its numbers suggest. The CVT was free of the rubber-band sensations other transmissions of this type can display, and its paddle shifters helped sharpen response in traffic or before a merge, providing a surprising degree of control. Direct, hefty steering and a firm, responsive brake pedal contributed to the almost sporty feel. Suspension tuning nicely balanced poise in corners and long-distance comfort. Road noise was fairly pervasive, though, detracting from the luxury credentials. Maybe that’s acceptable given the price. At under $46,000 fully loaded, the ADX tops out near where some rivals begin. Equipped to match the ADX, they easily cost thousands more. That makes the ADX a value play in the segment. Then again, it’s largely a luxed-up Honda HR-V with a stronger engine. It’s still somewhat loud, unsophisticated, and not especially distinctive. Even if you see panache in the Acura badge, accepting those similarities could be a reach. But as other upmarket automakers stuff their entry-level SUVs with dazzling doodads, annoying add-ons, and poseurish performance packages, the ADX takes a more predictable direction. That could appeal if you want to avoid the potential complications that come from owning an SUV from Acura’s competitors. The ADX isn’t dramatically better than an HR-V. Rather, it makes its case by being nicer in little ways. Here, any concern around the Honda connection comes down to perspective. It’s either too close to what everyone else drives or a strong basis for easy ownership. During my time with the ADX, I drove vehicles that put more emphasis on cutting-edge design, driver involvement, or absolute refinement. But returning to the ADX was always refreshing. Even if it never wowed me, it also never made me think twice about getting where I needed to go or doing what I needed to do. It just worked. And the extra layer of Acura polish smoothed out the daily grind. Is that the stuff of dreams? Perhaps not. That’s fine—the Acura ADX is built for reality. title: Daniel V. Hickey Obituary Nov 6, 2026 - Olson Funeral Home - Bloomer
content:
Daniel V. Hickey, age 86, of New Auburn, passed away peacefully on Friday, November 6, 2026, at Dove Rutledge Home in Chippewa Falls, under the care of Lily Hospice. Dan was born on March 24, 1940, in Tomahawk, WI to Vernon and Helen (Mason) Hickey. He attended Rhinelander High School and graduated with the Class of 1958. On December 27, 1986, Dan married Connie Demick in Bloomer, WI. He proudly served in the United States Marine Corps. After his service, Dan attended college at UW-Milwaukee where he ran track and earned a degree in physical education and geography. Upon graduation, Dan pursued an international career that took him to many places including Taipei, Taiwan and Cairo, Egypt, where he served as teacher, coach, athletic director and administrator. Upon return from overseas, Dan settled in New Auburn in 1979. He served as principal, then superintendent for the New Auburn School District for over 20 years. Additionally, Dan founded the New Auburn Syndrome Rugby Club where many people got to know him as a teammate, coach and mentor. Dan was a lifelong athlete, passionate about martial arts and rugby. Dan enjoyed sharing his passion for athletics with others, always bringing the same enthusiasm and commitment to every team and student. Upon retirement, Dan coached the UW–Stout Girls Rugby Team. He also had a keen interest in collecting firearms. Dan is survived by his wife: Connie Hickey; four children: Heather (Dan) Matthews of Florida, Kimberly Hickey of South Carolina, Don (Karen) Demick of Madison and John (Kerri) Hickey of Germantown; siblings: Patricia Donkle of Cambridge; five grandchildren; and numerous nieces, nephews, other relatives and friends. He was preceded in death by his parents: Vernon and Helen Hickey; and two brothers: Jerry and John Hickey. A celebration of life will be held from 1:00 to 3:00 PM, on Thursday, November 12, 2026, at the Bloomer Veterans Memorial, 1200 Veterans Memorial Dr. in Bloomer, with a time of sharing starting at 3:00 PM.
